source_locator.description: Opening parenthetical immediately after the canonical scene-1 heading.

translation.english_text: (As Kalyani's wedding is about to take place in Madurai, her three elder brothers—Chandrasekaran, Gnanasekaran and Gunasekaran—are in Rangoon. At that time, in Madurai... a dance is taking place at a gathering.)
notes: The three personal names are transliterated; the source relationship `அண்ணன்மார்கள்` is rendered as `elder brothers`.

Our prosperous Dravidian land. (Long live
Encircled by the southern sea, with Kumari dancing,
To the north extends Bengal, famed for valour;

notes: This is a semantic translation, not a singable adaptation; source line order is retained.
The compressed source form `பண்ணிகர்` is left untouched in Tamil and rendered contextually as `melodious` in English.
Source refrain fragments such as `(வாழ்க` / `(வாழ்கவே` are represented as `(Long live` cues rather than silently completed.

source_locator.description: Parenthetical after the opening song and immediately before Thangappan's speech.

translation.english_text: (When the dance and songs end, the bridegroom speaks.)

(Respected elders, until now you have enjoyed the voice of the new mingled with a new kind of dance. The children of such a beautiful land, instead of crawling in the lap of this Mother Earth, go away to other countries. When I think of this, I remember something one of our thinkers said. If we were to give an imaginative reason for why seawater is salty... he said it is because of the tears shed by Tamils who, unable to make a living in their own land, went abroad. Why go that far? Here is Kalyani, whom I am about to marry: she has apparently never even seen the faces of her brothers! They left for Rangoon when she was so young. And not only they! Hundreds of thousands of young people. Countless families! In Malaya's rubber plantations! In Africa, on the island of Ceylon—they must all return to our cherished homeland. That is exactly what this beautiful song reminds us of.)

source_locator.description: Opening direction after the scene-2 heading.

translation.english_text: (In Rangoon... Gnanasekaran enters while Gunasekaran is asleep.)
Little brother! Little brother, Gunasekara! Hey, wake up. Still sleeping? Get up, little brother—hey, Gunasekara! (Turns on the radio.) Hey, Kumbakarna, wake up!
notes: `Kumbakarna` retains the source's teasing mythological reference to a great sleeper.

translation.english_text: Mm... ayyo... my eyes! Coming and fooling around while I'm sleeping...
notes: `Ayyo` is retained as an exclamation.

source_locator.description: Chandrasekar enters.

translation.english_text: (At this moment Chandrasekar enters.)
What, have you two started already? Dawn has broken, hasn't it?
Brother, Gunasekaran only just woke up.
No, brother. I was up by five-thirty this morning.
Yes, yes—I'm the one lying.
notes: Sarcastic rendering of the compressed colloquial Tamil.

translation.english_text: Gnanasekara! Why are you lying? Our little brother doesn't even like seeing the sunrise. Mm... from home...
notes: The source trails off at `ஊரிலே இருந்து...`; the English remains incomplete.

translation.english_text: Has little sister's photograph arrived?
Father has written that little sister's marriage has been fixed!
Hey, look at that! When are all of us going home?
I've phoned and asked them to book the tickets. The reply should come any moment. (Goes over to sister-in-law.)
notes: The source direction `அண்ணியிடம் போதல்` leaves its grammatical subject implicit; the English therefore does not add a possessive such as `his`.

translation.english_text: Sister-in-law! Good news! Did you know Kalyani is getting married?
Sister-in-law would have been the first to know, wouldn't she? No, brother...!

source_locator.description: Chandrasekar looks at the photograph of Saraswathi's father and weeps.

translation.english_text: (Chandrasekar looks at a photograph of his wife Saraswathi's father and sheds tears.)
Little sister is getting married! Why have you suddenly become so upset?

No... when I saw your father's photograph, I felt strange; my whole mood changed. If he had been alive, how splendidly he would have conducted our wedding. It's just that he isn't here for this wedding now...
That's what your father is there for, isn't he?
Even so, he was the one who turned a ruined family into a prosperous one, wasn't he? From childhood we grew up under his protection. We played in his lap.

source_locator.description: The family sits down for coffee.

translation.english_text: (They sit down to drink coffee.)
(Looking at Guna.) Hey! Put that down. Coffee before you've even brushed your teeth?
Gnanasekara! You keep quiet. Go ahead, little brother.
notes: The source `சாப்பிடு` occurs in the coffee context and is rendered idiomatically as `go ahead`.

translation.english_text: What gift should we give Kalyani?
Our very hearts are beating for Kalyani. What better gift can we give than that? (The telephone rings.) Hello—Chandrasekaran speaking.
You asked for tickets, I hear?
Yes...
How many?
Four... four.
notes: The source code-switches with English `four`; the hesitation/repetition is preserved.

translation.english_text: Four won't be possible, sir!
It won't? Please, sir—somehow, try.
A great barrister—and how many 'pleases' do you have to say even for this?
Don't you know? Wartime...
Wartime, yes, sir! But this is an important marriage in our family! All of us absolutely have to go.
Only one person from a family is allowed. There are just three hundred seats in all. There's only one ticket...
All right, book it.
What is it, brother?

The ship leaving for Madras tomorrow has only three hundred tickets in all! And even then, only one person from each family. Our sister's golden occasion in life? We haven't been blessed with the chance for all of us to see it together.
notes: The unusual source phrase `தங்கையின் வாழ்விலே பொன் விழா?` is kept question-shaped rather than normalized into a more specific event label.

translation.english_text: Then who's going?
(Eagerly.) I'll go.

Gnanasekara, take the saris and jewellery our sister needs, put them in the trunk, and send them with Gunasekaran. (Gnanasekaran is saddened.) Gnanasekara, why are you worrying? We'll all be able to go.
Brother, what if the war situation becomes much worse by then?
Somehow we'll make it there.
I'll give half a dozen saris and blouses for Kalyani. Will there be room in the trunk?
It's for our sister—he'd carry it on his head if he had to. Just send it, sister-in-law.

source_locator.description: Closing direction after the final family exchange.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran departs.)

source_locator.description: Opening direction after the scene-3 heading.

translation.english_text: (In Madurai, Kalyani, dressed as a bride, stands before a mirror, weeping...)

Brother, have you forgotten me? I was not blessed with a mother to call 'Amma'; I thought at least I had you to call 'Anna.' They say that for a girl to be born with even one elder brother is a great sorrow; though I have three elder brothers, not one has come to see my wedding...
notes: The source sentence `உலகில் ஒரு அண்ணன் இருந்து பெண்ணைப் பிறந்தால் பெரும் துயர் என்பார்கள்` is semantically unusual; it is translated conservatively without silently repairing the Tamil.

translation.english_text: Kalyani! Don't cry, dear! It's the circumstances—it's happened to everyone... they'll come...
Circumstances? No—my fate.
Kalyani, don't be upset. Your brothers will come somehow. It's getting late; come.
Father, how many days I waited, thinking my brothers would come. Even now, not one brother has come to see me in my bridal attire?
They'll come, dear! If not today, they'll come tomorrow. Don't cry, dear.
Father, what if we postpone the wedding?
The priest fixed this day, dear. If we miss it, there'll be a dispute. Come—everyone is waiting.
notes: `ஐயர்` is rendered contextually as `the priest`; source metadata is not normalized.

source_locator.description: Closing direction after the final exchange.

translation.english_text: (The wedding takes place happily.)

source_locator.description: Opening direction after the scene-4 heading.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani and her husband rejoice, singing in refined Tamil in a grove where the cuckoo calls.)
notes: `பைந்தமிழ் பண்பாடி` is rendered as `singing in refined Tamil`; `மாங்குயில்` is rendered naturally as `cuckoo` rather than the overly literal compound `mango-cuckoo`.

english_lines: தங்: The lamp that kindles light in this life—
The form of the queen of my heart.
கல்: The one who shines as the flame within this lamp—
The form of the valiant one.
தங்: The form of a youthful peacock.
கல்: The lamp that kindles light in this life—
The lamp of our love.
தங்: O fruit! O sugarcane-sweet Tamil! O nectar!
O flower on which dew sleeps! O moon!
கல்: With your tender words, you have captivated me,
O magnetic statue.
தங்: When I see you, the feeling that wells within my heart—
There are no letters with which a writer could set it down.
இரு: Like this festive day, every day let us dance and sing,
And live as sweetly as honey. (In this life
notes: Semantic translation, not a singable adaptation.
Exact source speaker labels `தங்`, `கல்`, and `இரு` are retained inline.
The source refrain fragment `(இல்` remains incomplete in English rather than being reconstructed.
`இள மாமயில்` is rendered literally as `a youthful peacock`; no gendered substitution is introduced.

source_locator.description: Opening location marker after the scene-5 heading.

translation.english_text: [In Rangoon]

(Reading the newspaper.) The world war at its peak—Japan's war preparations! Enemies off the Rangoon coast; the ships have not reached India—brother, if Father and little sister hear this news, they'll be terribly upset. The wedding arrangements must be going on in full swing.
notes: The compressed source sequence around `இரங்கூன் கடலோரங்களில் எதிரிகள் கப்பல்கள் இந்தியா போய்ச் சேரவில்லை` is preserved conservatively; the English adds no causal claim absent from the Tamil.

translation.english_text: Yes. The ship Gunasekaran left on apparently still hasn't even reached Madras. We've become wretches unable to see our sister in her bridal attire.

source_locator.description: Radio war-news direction between the second and third dialogue records.

translation.english_text: [At this moment war news is broadcast on the radio. Today, enemy bombing caused heavy damage... about a thousand people were killed. An entire city in Burma has been emptied.]
How many more days can we go on living like this?
It feels as though simply escaping alive is a great struggle.
We shouldn't stay here any longer. Even if we have to walk, let's reach India.

source_locator.description: Closing direction after the decision to leave Rangoon.

translation.english_text: [They leave Rangoon on foot.]

source_locator.description: Opening location/character marker.

translation.english_text: [In Madurai, Kalyani and her husband Thangappan]
Kalyani!
Coming!
Mm... hurry up and get going.
notes: `புறப்படு சீக்கிரம்` is kept as a singular imperative; the earlier review wording `let's leave` added a first-person plural not present in the source.

translation.english_text: Why are you in such a rush? (As she comes out dressed, looking at her father.) Father, we're going out. We'll be back.......
notes: `ஏன் பறக்கிறீங்க` is rendered idiomatically as `why are you in such a rush`; the embedded source direction remains inside the dialogue unit.

translation.english_text: All right, dear. Go carefully and come back safely.

source_locator.description: Parvathi from the house opposite arrives.

translation.english_text: [At this moment Parvathi from the house opposite arrives.]
Kalyani...
Come in, sister.
I've come at just the right time... Where are you off to?
Nothing much. They're going to film a story written by the son-in-law, it seems.
Yes! For a long time Kalyani has been pestering me, saying she wants to watch a film being shot.
Of course she has to go. But does it look right for a woman in her condition to be going out like this at all hours?
notes: `முழுகாதிருக்கிற பெண்ணு` is a period/euphemistic reference to Kalyani's pregnancy; the English renders the contextual meaning as `a woman in her condition` rather than introducing a medical phrase absent from the source.

translation.english_text: It is wrong, but the child is eager to go. Let her go and come back.
notes: `குழந்தை` is retained semantically as an affectionate reference to Kalyani, not interpreted as the unborn child.

translation.english_text: It's only for today, sister!
Mm... go, dear, go! Son-in-law, keep listening to everything—just as you said! Once the boy comes, we'll have to rein her in.
notes: The source wording `மாப்புள்ளே நீ சொன்ன படியெல்லாம் கேட்டிரு` is colloquial/elliptical; the English deliberately does not supply the earlier review's unstated object `she`.
The final colloquial joke `பையன் வந்துல்ல அடக்கணும்` is rendered conservatively in its immediate pregnancy context.

translation.english_text: Oh, go on, sister.
Have you already decided it'll be a boy?
Whether I decide it or not, those two have apparently already decided—to name a boy Panneerselvam...
Not only that. If it's a girl, we've decided to name her Nagamma.

source_locator.description: Kalyani and Thangappan depart.

translation.english_text: (They leave.)
My daughter is clever indeed. If only my sons were here to see this happiness...

source_locator.description: Opening arrival direction.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran arrives in Madras, gets off the ship, and sits in a car.)
Sir...
notes: `சாமி` is rendered as the respectful address `Sir` in this begging context.

translation.english_text: All right, go on! What a fine first voice to hear in Tamil Nadu!... (He gives alms.)
notes: The line's irony on hearing a beggar as the `first voice` of Tamil Nadu is retained rather than explained away.
The source colloquial `சரிதாம்போ` is kept non-specific; the earlier review wording supplied `mother`, which is not explicit in the verified source text.

translation.english_text: Sir... I have children.
notes: `பிள்ளைக் குட்டிக்காரன்` states that the beggar has children/a family; the earlier review wording added `to feed`, which is contextual but not explicit.

translation.english_text: (When he has finished giving.) Driver, drive on.

source_locator.description: Bank, street pursuit, hotel and Jolly-in-room montage direction.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran drives to a bank. As he receives the money, a prostitute roaming the street sees it and follows him, poison in her heart. After collecting the money, he stays at a hotel. He asks the hotel manager to book a ticket, then returns to his room and enters. There—the young woman named Jolly, who followed him, is lying down. Seeing her, he...)
notes: The source's explicit term for the woman and its metaphor `நெஞ்சிலே நஞ்சுகொண்டு` are retained in meaning rather than softened.

translation.english_text: Forgive me! I came into your room by mistake. All the rooms look alike, so I couldn't tell the difference!
No problem! No problem. What's your room number?
Seven!—
Seven... mine is number eight. I'm the one who mistook the next room. (She pretends she is about to leave immediately.)
No problem! No problem. (A boy brings coffee.)
Have some coffee...
Mm... no... thanks.
Come on, have some. (He offers it.)
Mm... your... hometown?
I have to go to Madurai!—I missed the train.
Same with me.
I have to go to the cinema!... It's getting late.
(With distaste.) Cinema? Ugh! I don't like it one bit.
Why?

If an association were formed to shut it down, I'd be its president. Bharatanatyam dance is what suits our country. It would be so much better to go to that. I know a place with a good dance performance—come, let's go there.
notes: The source's English code-switches (`close`, `dance`) are rendered naturally without changing source metadata.

translation.english_text: (Surprised.) You too?
Why think of me differently like that? If I were your younger sister, wouldn't you take me along? Don't think wrongly of me like this.
All right, let's go.

source_locator.description: Opening dance-house direction.

translation.english_text: (With the playful Jolly beside him, Gunasekaran watches with distaste a dance taking place in a courtesan's house.)
notes: `தாசி வீடு` is rendered as `courtesan's house`; `ஜாலிக்காரி ஜாலி` carries a wordplay around Jolly's name that is only lightly reflected in English.

english_lines: O discerning gentleman, come!
Dressed in shining clothes,
Let us perform a joyous dance—when
We think of it, the heart
Sweetens; we know arts
That give delight and pleasure. (O discerning one
Seeing stone statues and paintings—and
Enchanted by their shapely beauty, by the sculpture's
Shapely beauty—do not, in vain,
Fill the mind with every fancy,
Rejoice in each as a marvel,
And sell away your reason—each day,
When you think of it, the heart
Sweetens; we know arts
That give delight and pleasure.
Seeking salvation in the heavenly world—millions
Have lost a life of pleasure—millions
Have lost the lives of women—merely
Standing in arrogance like a great sage,
Do not wander about in vain—each day,
When you think of it, the heart
Sweetens; we know arts
That give delight and pleasure.
notes: Semantic translation only; no singable metre or rhyme is introduced.
The source's compressed sequence around `பெண்களின் வாழ்க்கையை இழந்தவர்கள் கோடி` is translated conservatively rather than being silently rationalized.
The source refrain fragment `(ஓ ரசிகரும்` remains a cue rather than being reconstructed as a complete refrain.

source_locator.description: Jolly drugs Gunasekaran and takes his money.

translation.english_text: (At the dance performance, Jolly slips a stupefying drug into Gunasekaran's cold drink, renders him unconscious, and takes all his money.)

source_locator.description: Location shift to Kalyani's house.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani's house.)
(After examining Kalyani.) Get this medicine urgently and bring it back.
(Seeing his father-in-law coming toward him.) How is she now?
(Showing the doctor's prescription.) Get this medicine urgently and bring it back. (Thangappan rides away quickly on his bicycle.)
(Coming outside.) A grandson, Panneerselvam, has been born.
(Joyfully.) Son-in-law! Son-in-law!

source_locator.description: Closing deaths and widowhood direction.

translation.english_text: (The son-in-law, on his way to buy the medicine, is struck by a car opposite the house, falls, and dies. His father-in-law, Manickam Pillai, witnesses it and dies from the shock. Kalyani becomes a widow.)
notes: The verified source explicitly includes `விழுந்து` (`falls`); the second-pass English restores that action rather than compressing it away.

translation.english_text: Alas—I was deceived. After so many hardships I crossed the sea and came. Kalyani, this morning my hopes surged: I would see you, see my brother-in-law, see Father. Into my heart she poured poison... The deceitful woman, after fondling and flirting with me, has done me cruel harm; she might as well have killed me. A pauper... a wanderer—must I appear before my sister like this? Poverty, theft, deceit, prostitution! Where? In a country where unfailing life-giving rivers flow in abundance, on a land where fertile groves bloom and flourish! People unable to live, people who do not know a way to live, people born only to live! In this land, must every conceivable thing come upon me and torment me? O sacred land of lions! When did you become a spider's web? O prosperous Tamil land that gives life to those who come to you! How long have you been exploiting your own native sons? O my precious golden land, exalted again and again by chronicling the examples of heroic women! Why do you let prostitutes roam your streets and close your eyes? Why? Mansions touching the sky, people who have lost their honour; lofty towers... lowly hearts! O Tamil Nadu! Is this your greatness? Your worth? Your splendour? Kalyani!... you in Madurai... I on the streets of Madras! With a mind overturned and confused... orphaned, without support! Mute, unable to speak to anyone!... Ayyo... Kalyani... Kalyani.

The English page segments preserve the source break `நெஞ்சிலே / நஞ்சைக்` as an intentionally interrupted phrase.

source_locator.description: Opening Japanese bombing direction.

translation.english_text: (Chandrasekaran, his wife Saraswathi, and his younger brother Gnanasekaran are caught in a bombing by Japanese aircraft while on their way.)
notes: `குண்டுகளால் பாதிக்கப்படுகிறார்கள்` is kept broad as being caught/affected in the bombing; the English does not invent a specific wound or outcome here.

source_locator.description: Chandrasekaran and Saraswathi in hospital.

translation.english_text: (Chandrasekaran and Saraswathi are in the hospital.)
Doctor, sir... which bed is Gnanasekaran in?
notes: The source form `பெட்டிலே` is understood contextually as hospital `bed`; the Tamil remains unchanged.

translation.english_text: Gnanasekaran? There's no one by that name here.
Ah! Then where could he be?
These are the only people left from that bombing. Everyone else is dead.
Ah! Gnanasekara! Have you died? When Saraswathi goes home and Father asks, 'Where is Gnanasekaran?'—what answer will I give Kalyani?
notes: The source specifically says `சரஸ்வதி ஊருக்குப் போனவுடன்`; the English preserves Saraswathi as the grammatical subject rather than broadening it to `when we go home`.

translation.english_text: Doctor! Please say something to him.
Mr Chandrasekaran, don't trouble your mind. Stay calm.

source_locator.description: Creditors auction Manickam Pillai's house in Madurai.

translation.english_text: (In Madurai, creditors auction Manickam Pillai's house.)

This is to inform everyone that this house, number six, on Masi Konar Street, belonging to Manickam Pillai, will be sold by public auction tomorrow at three in the afternoon. This is an order of the court.
notes: The announcement's formal register and the source's house number, street and court-order details are retained without modernization.

translation.english_text: Hey, brother! Look at this misery... Trusting that his three sons in Rangoon were living in wealth and splendour, together like a bundle of bows, this poor Manickam Pillai borrowed money and celebrated his daughter's wedding lavishly—and the man himself died. Who knows what happened to those boys in the Japanese bombing of Rangoon? Well, leave that aside. Even after Kalyani used up the money she had and sold all her jewellery and ornaments, danger has now come even to the one house she had left... Mm... what else is going to happen?
notes: `வில்லுக்கொத்து போல` is translated conservatively as `together like a bundle of bows`; the source simile is retained rather than replaced with a smoother image.

The English avoids the impossible literal suggestion of `selling money`: `கையிலே இருந்த பணம், நகை நட்டையெல்லாம் விற்றுக்கொடுத்துக்கூட` is rendered as using up the money in hand and selling the jewellery while preserving the source sequence.

source_locator.description: Kalyani sits at the doorway with her child and sings through tears.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani, her face wet with tears, sits at the doorway holding the child and sings.)

english_lines: O flower-garland, you yourself—upon the dusty earth, in vain
I came; you crawled? (O flower-garland
Will you not look, my Panneerselvam?
We lived in prosperity; we fell, root and all.
The life we lived like a kingdom has fallen.
My king, were you born from this burdened womb of mine?
Why were you born? (O flower-garland
Even if you had been born in a bird's nest,
Food would have flown to you to drive away your hunger.
Crores upon crores of poor people live
In the land where the rich lords live—you were born there, my king.
Why were you born? (O flower-garland
notes: Semantic-poetic translation only; no singable metre, rhyme or completed refrain is introduced.

The verified source has the compressed/person-shifting form `வந்தேன் தவழ்ந்தாய்?`; the English deliberately preserves its first-person `I came` and second-person `you crawled?` rather than silently repairing the Tamil.
`பாரான எந்தன் வயிற்றில்` is semantically difficult; `this burdened womb of mine` is a contextual English reading recorded here, not a correction to the source.
The incomplete refrain cues `(பூமாலே` remain incomplete in English.

source_locator.description: Parvathi arrives after the song ends.

translation.english_text: (When the song ends, Parvathi arrives.)
Kalyani, what will become of you if every time I see you, you're like this—all tears and weeping? Look to what has to be done.
notes: `கண்ணீரும் கம்பலையுமாக` is rendered as the idiomatic pair `tears and weeping` without adding a diagnosis or emotional explanation.

translation.english_text: If someone comes forward to raise this child, then what has to happen will happen, won't it?
notes: The English does not specify what `நடக்க வேண்டியது` (`what has to happen`) refers to; the source leaves it implicit.

translation.english_text: What can the poor child do...
notes: `பாவம்` functions here as an expression of pity; it is not translated as an assertion that the child has committed a sin.

translation.english_text: Sister, the child isn't the sin! The great sin is being unable to raise this child in poverty.
notes: Kalyani's reply deliberately turns the preceding `பாவம்` into the stronger moral sense `sin`; the rhetorical contrast is retained.

translation.english_text: Kalyani! Listen to me. On the vacant plot we have at the edge of town, put up a small house. If you run an ordinary idli stall, surely you can make a living?
notes: `வயிறு வளர்க்க` is rendered idiomatically as `make a living`, retaining its subsistence sense.

translation.english_text: Ah! An idli stall?
In Tamil Nadu, for every woman whose tali has been cut, isn't that the Tahsildar's post?
notes: `தாலி அறுத்தவர்கள்` is a period expression for widowed women, literally those whose marriage tali has been cut/removed; the English preserves the source image rather than replacing it with a modern label.

`தாசில் உத்தியோகம்` is retained literally as `the Tahsildar's post`. The line is a sarcastic social comparison whose cultural force would be over-resolved by replacing it with a generic phrase such as `usual occupation`.

source_locator.description: Marwari shop location marker.

translation.english_text: (Marwari shop.)

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran struggles in Madras to find money to travel to Madurai.

translation.english_text: (Having lost his money in Madras, Gunasekaran struggles to find money to go to Madurai.)
Come, sir... what do you want? Tell me, sir?
notes: The shopkeeper's Tamil is deliberately marked by nonstandard/dialectal forms. The English conveys the meaning without inventing a caricatured accent; exact source wording remains in the Tamil record.

translation.english_text: Sir... I don't want anything. Will you buy these trousers from me?
This is very old! I'll give eight annas.
notes: `புராணு` is a dialectal/nonstandard source form understood contextually as `old`; the Tamil is not normalized.

translation.english_text: It's new, sir! I paid fifty rupees to have it stitched. I have to get to Madurai—at least give me enough for the train fare, sir.
You say—going to Bombay, going to Madras—what is that to me? I'll give eight annas.
notes: The source begins with the compressed dialectal form `நீப்பன்—`; the English keeps the shopkeeper's dismissive destination-listing without silently regularizing that Tamil form into a different word or place name.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran moves on and asks for money at a house.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran moves on. He goes to a house and asks for money.)
Ayyo! I came by ship—my money and trunk were all stolen.
notes: `பணம் பெட்டி` is kept as the source's compressed pair `money and trunk`; the English does not invent further details about the theft.

translation.english_text: If your money and trunk have been stolen, report it at the police station.
I have to get to Madurai—something...
notes: The source trails off after `ஏதாவது`; the English remains incomplete rather than supplying a request such as `give me something`.

translation.english_text: Go... go...

source_locator.description: At night Gunasekaran sleeps on a house platform and the householder pours water on him.

translation.english_text: (At night Gunasekaran is sleeping on a raised veranda. The householder brings water and pours it over him.)
notes: `திண்ணை` is rendered as `raised veranda`, retaining the architectural setting without adding action.

translation.english_text: Hey, you scoundrel! Who did you ask before coming and lying down here?
Sir... if there's a little more water, bring it and pour that too! It's been a long time since I bathed. Do you have a little soap?
You thieving fellow—(to his wife) Did you see his insolence?
Madam, you look like Lakshmi! If I were your younger brother, would you just stand there watching like this?
notes: The divine comparison `லட்சுமி மாதிரி` is retained as `like Lakshmi`; it is part of Gunasekaran's comic appeal.

translation.english_text: Did you see! The lout has come claiming a younger-brother relationship without any right to it!
notes: `தம்பி முறையில்லா கொண்டாட` uses kinship-language wordplay: Gunasekaran has claimed the relation `younger brother`, and she rejects that claim as having no proper relationship/right. The English preserves the social meaning rather than inventing a sexual implication.

translation.english_text: He'll claim it! Give him a little more time and he'll start claiming every relationship. You go inside first. (She goes inside.) (Looking at Gunasekaran.) Get out, get out...
notes: The repeated `கொண்டாடு` continues the preceding kinship-claim joke; the English keeps that connection.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran sleeps on a platform.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran goes and lies down to sleep on a raised veranda.)
notes: The source `திண்ணை` is rendered consistently as `raised veranda` in this scene.

translation.english_text: Hey, hey, hey, you lazy pickpocket! You've come and lain down after picking pockets, haven't you? What are you staring at?
If you wake a sleeping man, what else will he do but open his eyes?
notes: The reply preserves the wordplay on `முழிக்கிறே` / opening one's eyes rather than turning it into explanatory prose.

translation.english_text: Hey! You're a pickpocket, aren't you?
(Putting his hands into both pockets and feeling them.) No—empty pocket.
notes: The source's English code-switch creates the `pickpocket` / `empty pocket` joke; it is preserved directly.

translation.english_text: Then why did you come and lie down here?
Can't I even lie down here? Doesn't a human being have even the good fortune a cow has? Yes! In Madras, man is only a beast.
notes: `மாடு செய்த புண்ணியம்` is retained as the source's ironic comparison with a cow's `good fortune`; the English does not replace the metaphor with a modern rights-based formulation.

translation.english_text: Who are you talking about?

I'm not talking about you. With my spine breaking and breaking, I pull a handcart... in place of a horse, with my sinews straining and straining, I pull a rickshaw and become stooped; curled up like a dog, I live with my family on the pavement—that good man, that destitute one, I labour like a four-legged animal—I am talking about him. Madras is a sacred city! There, man is a beast.

english_page_segments.english_text: I'm not talking about you. With my spine breaking and breaking, I pull a handcart... in place of a horse, with my sinews straining and straining, I pull a rickshaw and become stooped—

curled up like a dog, I live with my family on the pavement—that good man, that destitute one, I labour like a four-legged animal—I am talking about him. Madras is a sacred city! There, man is a beast.

notes: The source uses repeated first-person verb forms (`இழுக்கிறேனே`, `வாழ்கிறேனே`, `உழைக்கிறேனே`) and then shifts toward third-person reference (`அந்த நல்லவன்... அவனை`). The English preserves that rhetorical instability instead of silently rewriting the whole passage into a consistent third person.
The source page break falls inside `போயிருக்கிறேனே`; the English page segments align the meaning at the nearest clause boundary rather than splitting an English word.

translation.english_text: When you become Mayor of Madras, all the beasts into men...
notes: The verified source itself ends the sentence fragmentarily at `மிருகத்தையெல்லாம் மனுஷனுக்கு.`. The English deliberately leaves the transformation clause incomplete rather than supplying a missing verb such as `turn` or `change`.

translation.english_text: Why... even now there are so many beasts in human form, aren't there?

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran leaves the place.

translation.english_text: (He moves away from that place.)

(Looking at the water tap.) Ah... at least God has shown me water! (No water comes.) Parasakthi, look at the fate of your son. He has no food to eat. No change of clothes to wear! No place to sleep! Parasakthi—
notes: The final `பராசக்தி—` remains an unfinished invocation, matching the source.

source_locator.description: Kalyani makes a living by running an idli shop in Madurai.

translation.english_text: (One day at Kalyani's home in Madurai, where she makes a living by running an idli shop—)
As of today it's come to three rupees. I'll pay tomorrow.

source_locator.description: The merchant who extended credit arrives.

translation.english_text: (At this moment the merchant who gave her credit arrives.)
Hey, Kalyaniamma! Kalyaniamma, if you have no way to repay it, why do you borrow?
Please wait two more days; as soon as the customers pay me, I'll pay you.
That won't do. (At this moment Venu arrives.)
notes: The Venu-arrival direction is embedded inside the immutable dialogue record and therefore remains inside this translation unit; no extra English endearment is added for the colloquial `ம்மா` ending.

translation.english_text: Hey! Who's that? Coming here and quarrelling with a woman who's alone? Can't you see a big man standing here?
notes: `பெரிய மனுஷன்` is kept as Venu's self-important `big man` rather than polished into a neutral `gentleman`.

translation.english_text: Maaf karo ji, Maharaj.
notes: The source code-switched phrase `மாப்கரோஜ் மகராஜ்` is transliterated rather than replaced, because Venu's next line plays on its sound.

translation.english_text: Maaf karo—rubbish! 'Roj'—how much is due?
notes: Venu mocks and breaks apart the preceding code-switched phrase (`மாப்கரோஜ்—மண்ணாங்கட்டி. ரோஜ்—...`). `Roj` is retained as sound-play; `மண்ணாங்கட்டி` is rendered idiomatically as the dismissive `rubbish` rather than explained away.

translation.english_text: Ten rupees.
Here you are. (He takes out money and gives it.)
Brother! You don't have to pay it.
It's all right! Go and bring idlis!

source_locator.description: Kalyani goes to bring idlis.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani goes to bring idlis.)
Is this how you come and make a scene with a woman who's alone, you shameless dogs!
notes: The source insult `வெட்கங்கெட்ட நாய்ங்க` is retained explicitly rather than softened.

translation.english_text: Why, Kalyani, do you borrow from people like this who have no sense of propriety?
notes: `தரந்தெரியா தவங்க` is colloquial/socially evaluative; `people ... who have no sense of propriety` preserves Venu's disparaging tone without assigning a modern class label not explicit in the source.

translation.english_text: What can I do, brother? I have to make a living.
notes: `வயிறு வளர்க்கணுமே` is rendered as the subsistence idiom `make a living`.

translation.english_text: Then do as I say—look, I've just paid ten rupees. Don't repay it in cash. Every morning give idlis to two people. I usually eat tiffin at night, so every night give me four annas' worth. Say that it will be deducted from these ten rupees. Later, as time goes on, once I see that you're trustworthy, I'll give you whatever money you need.
notes: `நாணயம்` is rendered contextually through `trustworthy`/creditworthiness, not as `coin`; the surrounding line concerns whether Venu can trust Kalyani with further money.

translation.english_text: Yes! It's poor people like this that we ought to help.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran, tormented by hunger, is on a platform in Madras like a madman.

translation.english_text: (In Madras, tormented by hunger, Gunasekaran is on a platform like a madman.)
Fruit... fruit... oranges... apples... fruit! Hey, do you want some fruit?
No, mother! I have no money.
notes: `அம்மா` is an ordinary respectful/familiar address here; `mother` preserves the source address without asserting a family relation.

translation.english_text: No money? Then here—keep an eye on this! I'm going to drink some water and come back.
notes: `இதைப் பார்த்துக்கோ` is rendered contextually as `keep an eye on this`, referring to the basket she is about to leave; no extra action is added.

source_locator.description: The fruit seller leaves her basket; Gunasekaran takes and eats fruit without asking.

translation.english_text: (She leaves the fruit basket and goes. Without asking the fruit seller, Gunasekaran takes a fruit and eats it.)
Hey! Hey—why did you take my fruit?
The cruelty of hunger, mother!
notes: The compressed source `பசிக் கொடுமையம்மா` is kept forceful rather than expanded into an explanation.

translation.english_text: Because you're hungry, does that tell you to steal and eat, you wretch?... I toil and suffer, roam four streets to earn a few coins, and you've come to snatch that away?
If I were your son, wouldn't you forgive me? [para-2]
notes: The verified source ends with the unexplained token `பாரா-2`. It is retained transparently as `[para-2]` rather than guessed away or assigned a meaning.

translation.english_text: God himself should question you.
He hasn't heard my cry of anguish, mother; his heart has turned to stone.
All my fruit has gone to waste! At which Mariamman temple shall I scoop up earth and fling it for you? Hey, if you don't put down the money properly, I'll break your teeth.
notes: `மண்ணைப் போச்சே` is rendered idiomatically as `gone to waste`; the following Mariamman-temple line remains the source's ritual/cursing image rather than being replaced with a generic modern curse.

translation.english_text: Where am I to get money, mother? If you want, I'll carry this fruit and sell it for you without wages.
Sell it, you good-for-nothing? Look at your face! Hey, you've eaten the fruit, peeled it, and put the skin right back in there? Lift it! Hey, lift it!
notes: The opening `வித்தாத்தானே வீணுப்போனவனே?` is colloquial and compressed; `Sell it, you good-for-nothing?` preserves the immediate challenge without adding a fuller explanation absent from the source.

source_locator.description: A madman knocks over the fruit basket, takes fruit, is chased by police and frightens them off; Gunasekaran watches.

translation.english_text: (At this moment a madman comes, knocks over the fruit basket, takes fruit and runs. The police chase him, but he threatens the police themselves and goes away. Seeing this, Gunasekaran...)

Mad world. In this world, is it only the man who goes about deceiving others who can survive? Did I steal to buy a dhoti? Or to build a house? Unable to bear my stomach's hunger, I stole one fruit... the reward for it: blows, kicks, abuse. A madman steals a bunch of fruit. The world is afraid of him. It forgives him. From now on, we too can survive only if we adopt another way.
notes: The sequence `அடி, உதை, திட்டு` remains the blunt three-part `blows, kicks, abuse`; Gunasekaran's social inference is not softened or moralized in English.

source_locator.description: A woman passes on the road; two minors watch her walk.

translation.english_text: (At this moment a woman walks along the road. Two young men watch the beauty of the way she walks.)
notes: The exact source term `மைனர்` remains preserved in speaker metadata. The stage direction uses `young men` to avoid the misleading modern English age-sense of `minors` without inventing a new class label.

translation.english_text: Her walk has a beauty all its own, sir! If only we could get a figure like that!
notes: The source objectification in `இந்த மாதிரி உருவப்படி நமக்குப் கிடைக்கணுமே` is retained rather than rewritten into more modern social language.

translation.english_text: Anything can be had if you put down money, sir...

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran beats the minors.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran beats the two young men.)
notes: The English follows the scene's reviewed rendering of `மைனர்கள்` as `young men`; exact Tamil labels remain unchanged in source metadata.

translation.english_text: Cigarette... (The minors give it to him.) Ha... ha... Lux. (From today, I too am a cheat.)
notes: The source code-switch/brand-like form `லக்ஸ்` is retained as `Lux` without assigning a product or additional action not stated in the source. The embedded source direction is kept close to its wording; exact source labels remain unchanged.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran learns from the madman that a cheat can survive, pretends madness and collects money while dancing and singing.

translation.english_text: (Having learned from the madman the lesson that only a cheat can survive, Gunasekaran too pretends to be mad, dances and sings, and extorts money from many people.)
notes: `பட்டம் பயின்ற` is rendered as `learned ... the lesson`; the direction's explicit `பணம் பறிக்கிறான்` is retained as `extorts money` rather than softened to voluntary collection.

english_lines: Nation, wisdom, learning, and worship of God—all of them
Do not prevail before money, Kudambai;
Do not prevail before money.
God himself and the worship of God, in this land,
Come behind money—Kudambai;
Come behind money.
Once the visible money has left the hand,
No witness will go up to court.
Those with bags upon bags of gold,
Even if they tell lie after lie,
It passes as truth upon truth—Kudambai;
It passes as truth upon truth.
Even if he is a good man, one who has nothing
The country will not respect—Kudambai, the country will not respect.
That the learned celebrate an uneducated fool—
It is silver money, Kudambai;
It is silver money.
notes: This is occurrence `parasakthi-song-005`, the `குதம்பாய்` section of soundtrack track 1. It remains separate from the following `தாண்டவக்கோனே` occurrence because the verified Tamil derivative preserves them as structurally distinct source sections.
Semantic-poetic translation only; no rhyme, metre or new refrain is introduced.
`காட்சியான பணம்` is rendered conservatively as `visible money`; the unusual source wording is not silently rationalized.
`சாட்சி கோர்ட்டு ஏறாதடி` is kept in its literal courtroom image as `No witness will go up to court` rather than expanded into a legal explanation.

english_lines: Even if you dance an Aryan dance,
O Tandavakkone—on matters of money,
Keep your eye open, O Tandavakkone.
Keep enmity inside,
O Tandavakkone—for money,
Keep kinship on your lips, O Tandavakkone.
Every fool, O Tandavakkone—money
Makes into a master, O Tandavakkone—money.
When you embrace and weep,
O Tandavakkone—the corpse.
When you embrace and weep, O Tandavakkone—keep your eye
On the money-box, O Tandavakkone.
notes: This is occurrence `parasakthi-song-006`, the `தாண்டவக்கோனே` section of the same soundtrack composition as `parasakthi-song-005`; it remains a separate translation unit because the verified source derivative identifies it separately.
`ஆரியக் கூத்து` is translated literally as `Aryan dance` without adding historical or ideological explanation inside the lyric.
The source's compressed syntax and split around `பணப் / பெட்டிமேலே` are kept semantically close; no singable rewrite is attempted.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran, pretending to be mad, reaches Madurai near his locked home and questions Parvathi nearby.

translation.english_text: (Pretending to be mad, Gunasekaran comes from Madras to Madurai and reaches the neighbourhood of his home. Finding the house locked, he questions Parvathi, who is standing nearby giving alms.)
Hey! Who are you? Wait, I'm coming.
No, mother, I'm not a beggar. There was a man named Manickam Pillai in the next house—where is he now, mother?
Who? Kalyani's father, isn't it?
Yes, mother!
He died.
Ah... he died? Then his daughter Kalyani?

Kalyani! She's like a daughter to me too! She was like a finely carved statue. Her wedding all went well. That accursed god did not let her have a life either... The following year, it made her a widow with an infant in her arms!
notes: `கடைஞ்செடுத்த சிலைமாதிரி` is retained as the image of a finely carved statue.
`பாழும் தெய்வம்` is rendered as the lamenting `accursed god`; the English does not add a theological explanation.
`சிசுவும் கையுமா` is rendered contextually as `with an infant in her arms`.
Second-pass review tightened `மறுவருஷம்` from the looser `the year after` to `the following year`.

translation.english_text: Ah, ayyayyo... where is Kalyani now, mother?
There, at the end of that street, she runs an idli stall. You're grieving so much—who are you?
Even if I told you who I am, you wouldn't know me, mother.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran goes to the house at the end of the street in search of Kalyani.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran goes to the house at the end of the street in search of Kalyani.)

source_locator.description: Kalyani sings to her child in the cradle while Gunasekaran watches in deep sorrow.

notes: `கண்கள் கடலாக` is retained as the source's ocean image rather than expanded into an explicit statement about tears.
translation.english_text: (Kalyani lays her child in the cradle and sings. Watching her, Gunasekaran stands with his eyes an ocean, sorrow piercing his heart.)

notes: Semantic-poetic translation only; no singable metre or rhyme is introduced.
`மாமன்மார் மூவர் தம்பி` is read with `தம்பி` as an address to the child (`little one`), not as an invented fourth kinship relation.
`பாலாடை` is rendered as an infant `feeding cup`; the source's jewel imagery is kept without modernizing the object.
`சீதனம்` is retained as `seethanam` because the lullaby presents it as a maternal uncle's ceremonial gift; the English does not narrow it to a modern legal sense of dowry.
Second-pass review tightened the opening images while preserving their source order and the PDF 21→22 occurrence boundary.
english_lines: O parrot that speaks tender words—O flourishing
Delicate lotus flower—O
Guileless full moon, good nectar
Risen in the sky of joy!
My dear, my precious one, will you not sleep?
Your three maternal uncles, little one—will come
To give you a good life.
They will come to shower kisses
Upon your mango-like cheek.
My dear, my precious one, will you not sleep?
A ruby feeding cup—with an emerald
Cradle—and a silver elephant
As your vehicle—the youngest uncle
Will give them as seethanam.
My dear, my precious one, will you not sleep?
On a tablet made of silver—with a fine
Diamond stylus,
To write lessons in clear Tamil, your uncle
Will come to enroll you in school—your uncle
Will come to gather you into his arms.
My dear, my precious one, will you not sleep?

source_locator.description: The meaning of the song multiplies Gunasekaran's sorrow.

translation.english_text: (The meaning of the song multiplies his sorrow many times.)

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran's unlabelled conscience text after the lullaby.

notes: The source block is unlabelled and explicitly identifies itself as Gunasekaran's conscience. It is source-located here without inventing a dialogue-record ID.
translation.english_text: Yes. The maternal uncles will come in splendour... Kalyani, I must not destroy your cherished dream. In this madman's disguise, you need not recognize me at all—(This is Gunasekaran's conscience.)

notes: `சுமைதாங்கி` is a roadside load-rest/load-bearer. The English preserves the source wordplay `சுமைதாங்கி / சோகம் தாங்கி` as `bearer of burdens / bear my sorrow` rather than replacing it with an unrelated image.
translation.english_text: Wouldn't it have been better if the ship that lost its course at sea had simply capsized? Kalyani, did I come running with such eagerness only to see you in this state? (He goes near the roadside load-rest.) O bearer of burdens, from now on you will bear my sorrow! This is my home! My life is here! My occupation is to follow Kalyani like a shadow.

source_locator.description: The young men are playing cards.

notes: The source calls them `மைனர்கள்`; the English avoids standalone `minors`, whose modern age-sense can mislead. Exact source labels remain unchanged in dialogue metadata.
translation.english_text: (The young men are playing cards.)
Turn it over, man.
Three kings, brother.
If only I had three aces...

notes: The source form `லாண்டறி` is treated as the English loan `laundry`; the joke remains source-dependent and is not further rationalized.
translation.english_text: You'd open a laundry.
Why are you laughing? I'm the one who's not joining the game.

notes: `ஆள் அவுட்டா` is rendered conservatively as being `out` of the game; the source's card-table register is retained.
translation.english_text: What, are you out? Just stay, man—we can win back all the money we've lost.

notes: The verified source form `டேபின்` is lexically unclear. It is retained transparently as `tebin` rather than assigned an unsupported denomination or object.
translation.english_text: But even for that we need money! Hey... if you had it, wouldn't you give me some? Hey, just give me one tebin.

notes: The Hindi code-switch `பைசா நஹி` is retained as `Paisa nahi` rather than flattened into standard English.
translation.english_text: Paisa nahi! What, man... your father has given you the key to the iron safe, and you're afraid...

notes: The period colloquial `காக்கா வலிப்பு` denotes a fit/seizure expression. Second-pass review keeps the English generic as `fits` rather than imposing a more specific modern diagnosis or reproducing the literal crow-image.
translation.english_text: It's only the key... I often get fits; that's why he gave it to me.
Hey—are you coming there? Let's go...
Where?

source_locator.description: The young man is taken away by Venu.

notes: The source uses `மைனர்`; `young man` avoids the misleading modern English legal/age sense of `minor`.
translation.english_text: [The young man is led away by Venu.]

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran deliberately babbles as though mad.

translation.english_text: [He is deliberately babbling as though mad.]

notes: The source's mock-royal register and onomatopoeic `டுமீர்` are retained rather than normalized into realistic court dialogue.
translation.english_text: Did he teach us to boil stones and earth... and drink them? (He laughs.) I am the Maharaja myself—no doubt about it! Who are they? Ministers and chief ministers, come! Sit on this seat! Let the Bharatanatyam begin—dumeer, dumeer, dumeer!

source_locator.description: Unlabelled Gopalan/Nandagopalan verse performed by Gunasekaran.

notes: The source block is unlabelled and is not a verified soundtrack occurrence. Scene context places it inside Gunasekaran's performed babbling, so it is source-located as dialogue-like performance without inventing a song occurrence ID.
Second-pass review treats the source line-end forms `நந்த / கோபாலன்` and `வேணு / கோபாலன்` as split name forms (`Nanda-gopalan`, `Venu-gopalan`) rather than implying the character Venu.
english_lines: With Gopalan I will dance—with Nanda-
gopalan I will dance—with Venu-
gopalan—ah, Nandagopalan—oo, Nanda-
gopalan;
Like a cuckoo of music I will dance.

source_locator.description: Unlabelled mock-royal, political and devotional performance by Gunasekaran.

notes: This source block is unlabelled but occurs inside Gunasekaran's deliberate madman performance; it is source-located without inventing a dialogue-record ID.
`மாதம் மும்மாரி மழை` retains the idealized `three times a month` rain formula rather than being modernized.
The verified source forms `கடக்கட்டு` and `வாட் வசிக்குதா?` are semantically opaque. They are exposed as `kadakkattu` and `What—vasikkudha?` rather than silently assigned invented meanings.
`பவுன் விளையுற நாடு` is rendered as a land where gold sovereigns grow; `பரதேசி` is retained as `paradesi` in the source's insulting/social register.
The code-switched English-like forms (`வேர் யு ஆர்`, `வாட் யு வாண்ட்`) remain deliberately nonstandard in English, reflecting the source performance.
The closing devotional chant is transliterated conservatively from the verified Tamil rather than standardized from an external liturgical source.
Second-pass review changes the looser `realm` to source-nearer `nation` for `தேச விசாரணை`.
translation.english_text: Ayyo! Ayyo! Enough, enough! Let the inquiry into the nation begin—dum, dum, dum! Minister, does rain fall three times a month in our great city? Dumeer! Dumeer! That's why we've tied a 'kadakkattu' for Lord Varuna and sent a telegram, Maharaja! Bravo, bravo! Who are they? Why are they shouting? Oi, oi, Maharaja, we cannot bear the hunger in our bellies—we are dying, family after family. What—vasikkudha? Don't say that, sinner! This is a land where gold sovereigns grow! You paradesi fellows, are you starving? Die—die happily! Only then will the comet rise. Sir—sir—r, Maharaja, no money? Where you are! What else you want? Carry kavadi for Vadamalaiyan—For Vadamalaiyan... (He picks up a brick.) Arohara! Sarvarama Sanjeevi Nama Parvatham, Rama Sankeerthanam... Govinda... Hare Govinda!

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran places the brick on the roadside load-rest.

translation.english_text: (He places the brick on the roadside load-rest.)

source_locator.description: Unlabelled planted-stone verse performed by Gunasekaran.

notes: The source does not attribute this verse and the verified song inventory does not classify it as a soundtrack or quoted-verse occurrence. It therefore remains a scene-located unlabelled performance unit; no external authorship is introduced.
`நட்டகல்` is retained literally as a `planted stone`; the rhetorical attack on ritual is not softened.
english_lines: You call a planted stone a god and deck it with four flowers;
You circle it, muttering and muttering—what mantra is that?
Will the planted stone speak when the Lord is within?
Can a fired pot and ladle know the taste of the curry?

source_locator.description: Unlabelled bhajan refrain performed by Gunasekaran.

notes: The refrain is unlabelled in the scene and is not a verified soundtrack occurrence. It remains a scene-located performance unit rather than being promoted into the song inventory.
english_lines: Let us sing bhajans, Kannan's name, while starving;
Let us sing bhajans, Kannan's name.
Let us sing bhajans, Kannan's name—while starving;
Let us sing bhajans, Kannan's name.

source_locator.description: Kalyani sees Gunasekaran speaking in many guises like a madman.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani sees Gunasekaran, who in this way speaks in many guises like a madman.)
Ayyo—poor thing—it seems someone here is mad.
Little sister, little sister, come here.
What? So I'm your little sister?
Yes! For two or three days I've been thinking of telling you something.
What?

notes: The source has the male Gunasekaran absurdly promise `நான் ஒரு பொண்ணு பெத்து தர்றேன்`; the English preserves the madman proposal rather than rationalizing it as finding someone else's daughter.
translation.english_text: Nothing... I'll have a daughter—will you arrange for her to marry your son?

notes: `சீதனம்` is rendered as `dowry` here because Kalyani explicitly answers the proposed marriage arrangement; this differs from its broader ceremonial-gift sense in the scene-17 lullaby.
translation.english_text: All right—what about the dowry?
We can see about that later. First, let me hold my 'son-in-law' for a moment—I'll give him a kiss and hand him back.
Ayyo—I won't.

notes: The closing source form `தாளா துயரத்தோடு` is compressed; `with unbearable sorrow` is a contextual English rendering, not a Tamil correction.
translation.english_text: Little sister, just once! Won't you let me hold him? Little sister, I swear—I'm not mad. I won't harm your child. Won't you let me hold him? Yes, I am mad. (He goes away with unbearable sorrow.)

source_locator.description: Compressed location marker: road.

notes: The verified source has the compressed form `இடம்ரோடு`, read as a location marker rather than silently altering the Tamil.
translation.english_text: (Location: road.)
Vadai! Murukku! Sir! Do you want murukku?
Give me three annas' worth.

notes: `போணி` is the trader's first/auspicious sale; it is rendered contextually as `first sale` rather than retained as unexplained jargon.
translation.english_text: Good God! It's been three days since I've made a first sale. How much vadai and how much murukku?

notes: The source embeds `(கொடுக்கிறான்)` inside Gunasekaran's record; context makes the vendor the giver, but the Tamil record itself remains unchanged.
translation.english_text: Give me this for two annas and that for one anna, man! (The vendor gives it.)
Your hand works all right, doesn't it?

notes: The English preserves the source pun on `நடக்கு`, which can mean both `work/function` and `walk`.
translation.english_text: A hand doesn't walk—the leg walks. (He shows this with a gesture.)
Ayyo—poor thing, you seem very hungry. Eat, eat!
Hey... murukku.
Wait, I'll get the money from this gentleman. Take out the money, man—mm—take it out—
(He laughs.)
Why are you laughing, man?
(He laughs again.)
Hey! Why are you laughing again? Take out the money; I have four streets to cover.

notes: Second-pass review corrects the earlier mistaken `pick what up?` reading. `பொறுக்கவா?` directly asks whether the vendor is going around to scavenge/pick things up.
translation.english_text: Why—to scavenge?
Who is this insolent fellow? I said take out the money.
Hey!—Money? For you? What for?

notes: `மாமா மச்சான் மாதிரி` invokes familiar kinship terms; the English retains the source relation pair rather than replacing it with a generic `friends`.
translation.english_text: Why are you fooling around as though we're uncle and brother-in-law? Are you trying to cheat me? Who do you think I am!
Then give me another two annas' worth.
Now you're talking! Here, take it. (He gives it; Gunasekaran eats.) Take out the money—mm—it's getting late.
(Like a madman.) Ah, you fellow—

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran drives the vendor away, lifts the box himself and leaves with it.

translation.english_text: (He drives the vendor away, picks up the box himself and sets off.)
Boss, do you want murukku?
Is it hot?
Both are.
Then give me one anna's worth of this and one anna's worth of that.
Take out the money.
Hey, give it first.
Sir, will two annas' worth be enough for you?

notes: `ஓசி` is rendered as `extra for free`, preserving the bargaining sense rather than translating it as a named item.
translation.english_text: Not enough! One shouldn't spend too much money. Since I'm buying for two annas, give me a little extra for free.
Ayyo, even here you haven't lost your beggar's mentality! Here, have this free. (He breaks off a little and gives it.) Take out the money.
Money? Do you have change for a rupee?
What?
Do you have change for one rupee?

notes: The source shifts abruptly from taking the rupee to the mock question `ஏதுங்காணும் இந்தக் காசு?`; the English preserves that comic discontinuity rather than rationalizing the trick.
`கொண்டாடா` is read contextually as the colloquial command to hand/bring the rupee over; the verified Tamil form is left untouched.
translation.english_text: Change? From me? You fool, hand it here. (He takes the rupee and holds it in his hand.) What a chance—would I let this slip? What is this money, sir?
What, sir—this money?

notes: The source code-switch `எய்ட் நாட்திரீ` is rendered phonetically as `eight nought three`.
The verified source word `கொட்டாபுளி` is semantically unclear in this context and is retained transparently as `kottapuli` rather than assigned an unsupported insult or object.
translation.english_text: Hey, 'eight nought three'—take this kottapuli away! [He runs off with the rupee.]
Fine—the box is still here, isn't it?

source_locator.description: The vendor returns for the box; the proprietor resists; the box is put on his head and police make an arrest.

notes: The final source `பிடித்துக்கொண்டு போதல்` does not explicitly name which man the police take. The English retains the source's pronoun-level ambiguity rather than specifying which person is taken.
translation.english_text: [The vendor comes and lifts the box... The proprietor refuses to let him take it. The vendor lifts the box and puts it on the proprietor's head; at once the police arrive, seize him and take him away.]

source_locator.description: Venu, driven by lust, knocks at Kalyani's door with predatory intent.

translation.english_text: [Venu, a black cobra seized by lust, knocks at Kalyani's door intending to taste the fruit that is Kalyani.]
notes: The source itself uses the predatory metaphors `கருநாகம்` (black cobra) and `கனி` (fruit); the English retains them rather than neutralizing the stage direction.

translation.english_text: Kalyani!
[On opening the door.] Why, brother, so late? From now on, come earlier.
I've come at just the time I should, haven't I? Why, Kalyani, how was business today?
Same as always today too.
Mm... there are idlis, aren't there?
Wait, brother! I'll bring them.
Why, Kalyani! At a time when rice is hard to get, instead of making them entirely with rice like this, what if you mixed in a little wheat—
We can, but the taste will be spoiled.
Anything is better as two than alone. If the wheat joins in too, the profit will be greater, won't it!
notes: Venu's shift from food adulteration to `two rather than alone` carries an insinuating double meaning; the English keeps the source wording broad enough for that turn.

translation.english_text: Can we do wrong for profit, brother?
Why do you say 'brother' thirty-two times with every breath?
notes: `மூச்சிக்கு முப்பத்திரண்டு` is a comic hyperbole; the second-pass English keeps `thirty-two` while making the repeated-address construction explicit rather than saying she `puts` brothers into a breath.

translation.english_text: Brother! I have three elder brothers. I became a sinner not blessed to see even one of them! Out of longing, at least I call you brother, brother...
You fool, if the longing is so great, is calling me 'brother, brother' the answer?
notes: Venu deliberately twists Kalyani's familial `ஆசை`/longing into his sexualized line of talk; the English does not resolve the word into a single modern sense.

translation.english_text: Brother! There's something improper in your talk, isn't there?
That is a way of showing desire, Kalyani!
Brother, speaking like this to women who are alone—
Yes! A tender vine shouldn't be alone—that's why I'm here as a jackfruit tree fit for it to climb. Call me 'mama'! What a charming word! Call me 'athan'! What a substantial word.
notes: The source switches among kinship terms `அண்ணா`, `மாமா`, and `அத்தான்` as part of Venu's insinuation. `mama` and `athan` are retained transliterated so the kinship-wordplay is not falsely mapped to one English family relation.
The source form `மாழி` is left untouched in Tamil; the English reads the phrase contextually as referring to the word/expression.

translation.english_text: Stop! I can't bear any more.
What life is there here! It's the same for me too—just say yes. Where there is a thatched hut, I'll build you an upper storey. Kalyani who slept on a ragged mat will sleep on a golden-jewelled bed.
notes: The opening `இங்கே என்ன வாழுதாம்! தானும் அப்படித்தான்` is compressed/colloquial; the English remains conservative rather than supplying a more specific proposition.

translation.english_text: Chi! Don't come near me! How many of you have set out like this thinking women suffering in poverty will fall if you cast a deceitful net?
Lamentation on a battlefield! Wailing in a field of pleasure—those are the acts of cowards, my delicate lady.
notes: The source contrasts `போர்க்களம்` with `போகக் களம்`; `field of pleasure` keeps the sexualized rhetorical contrast without adding a new metaphor.

translation.english_text: If you try to touch me, I'll shout.
Shout! Let your shout be music to me.

source_locator.description: Venu embraces Kalyani and attempts to kiss her; Gunasekaran arrives.

translation.english_text: [Saying this, the lust-mad scoundrel Venu embraces Kalyani and is about to taste her red lips. At this moment Gunasekaran arrives...]
notes: The source uses `செவ்விதழைச் சுவைக்க` (`taste her red lips`) and explicitly characterizes Venu as lust-driven; the English preserves that source framing without adding action beyond the attempted assault.

translation.english_text: No need for courtesy, da, brother-in-law! [He beats Venu and drives him away.]
notes: `மைத்துனு` is retained as the taunting kinship address `brother-in-law`; the beating direction is embedded in the immutable dialogue record.

translation.english_text: If you hadn't come, what would have happened to me! Crazy brother, how did you come here?
notes: `கிறுக்கண்ணா` is Kalyani's address to the apparently mad Gunasekaran; `crazy brother` preserves both the madness label and `அண்ணா` kinship address.

translation.english_text: Just to see you.
Crazy brother, what have you been doing under that tree for ten days?
Running a kingdom.
Crazy brother, I'll give you idlis. Will you eat?
Mm... you'll ask me for money.
No money needed.
If I tell you who I am, you won't ask for money at all.
Who are you?
I... I am the Maharaja under the tree!
I'll bring idlis.
No... no, amma... I don't want idlis, amma... I want chutney, amma...
notes: The repeated `-ம்மா` is a feminine vocative here; the second-pass English retains it transparently as `amma` instead of the misleading literal kinship `mother`.

translation.english_text: All right, I'll bring both. (She goes.)

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran goes behind and kisses the child sleeping in the cradle; tears fill his eyes.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran goes around to the back and kisses his 'son-in-law', who is asleep in the cradle. There are tears in his eyes.)
notes: The source calls the child `தன் மாப்பிள்ளை`; the English retains `son-in-law` in quotation marks rather than silently replacing the source kinship joke/usage.

translation.english_text: (With the idlis.) Why are you crying, crazy brother?
Mm...... all the subjects in my kingdom are happy... and among them, I am crying.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran drops the rupee in his hand onto the idli plate and leaves.

translation.english_text: (Saying this, he drops the rupee in his hand onto the idli plate and leaves.)
Crazy brother! Crazy brother!
notes: The source uses `!` rather than the usual colon after the explicit label `கல்`; the immutable dialogue record preserves that anomaly and the translation keeps the exact label metadata.

source_locator.description: The next morning some young men gossip in front of a shop while Gunasekaran brushes his teeth nearby.

translation.english_text: (The next morning, some young men stand gossiping in front of a shop. Near them, Gunasekaran is brushing his teeth. Then—)
notes: The source uses `மைனர்கள்`; the English stage direction uses `young men` to avoid the misleading modern age/legal sense of `minors`, while exact dialogue labels remain unchanged.

translation.english_text: Where were you, man? Didn't see you all night.
Cards all night—my eyes are burning!
So your eyes burned! Did you at least get any money? Mm... that's exactly what you didn't.
Where's Venu? Can't see him anywhere.
The man's gone to lie on a soft bed. You know that idli seller Kalyani! Our fellow wagged his tail at her... his scheme didn't work... poor fellow got a good beating.
notes: `வால் ஆட்டியிருக்கான்` is retained as the animal-image `wagged his tail`; `பாச்சா பலிக்கலே` is rendered conservatively as his scheme not working rather than assigned a more specific game or trick.

translation.english_text: Hey, keep quiet! Why are you flapping your mouth for nothing too? Some fellow wandering around in a madman's disguise is also Kalyani's illicit lover...
notes: The colloquial `ஒட்டையை வீணு அலட்டிக்கிட்டே?` is rendered as idle mouth-flapping/chatter; the Tamil is not normalized.
`கள்ளப்புருஷன்` is translated explicitly as `illicit lover`, preserving the defamatory force that triggers Gunasekaran's reaction.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran hears the slander and becomes angry.

translation.english_text: (Hearing this, Gunasekaran becomes enraged.)
(Beating the young men.) What did you say—a stain on my Kalyani? Kalyani is my sister, my sister! I'm going right now to tell her who I am.
notes: The beating action is embedded inside the immutable dialogue record; it therefore remains inside this translation unit.
`களங்கம்` is retained as the source's stain/disgrace image rather than expanded into a more specific accusation.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran runs furiously toward his sister's house.

translation.english_text: (He runs furiously toward his sister's house.)

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran does not find Kalyani in the hut.

translation.english_text: (Not finding Kalyani in the hut.)
Circumstance made my sister a widow; society did not let her live. (Not finding Kalyani, he turns back. On the way...)
notes: The source's paired accusation `சந்தர்ப்பம்... சமுதாயம்...` is kept as `circumstance... society...`; the embedded return direction remains within the dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Sir, around here, a widow with a child...
Hey, is that a woman you know? Go look over there in that crowd. She committed suicide.
Ah—Kalyani! (He learns that the dead woman there is not Kalyani and returns.)

source_locator.description: Kalyani gives up her idli business in Madurai and leaves the town.

translation.english_text: [Kalyani gives up her idli business in Madurai and leaves the town altogether.]

source_locator.description: Chandrasekar, having left Rangoon, is a judge in Tiruchi under the name M. C. Sekar.

translation.english_text: (Chandrasekar, having left Rangoon, is now a judge in Tiruchi under the name M. C. Sekar.)
Did you get any information?
Not a single piece of information!
Yes—do they know you've come to this town?
No!
In any case, shall we go and see them in person?
Yes. That's why I asked them to come. We'll leave tomorrow itself.
notes: The source sequence is preserved without reconciling its travel logic.

source_locator.description: Black-market dealer Narayana Pillai counts the goods he has hoarded.

translation.english_text: [Black-market scoundrel Narayana Pillai counts what he has hoarded.]
notes: The pejorative `கள்ள மார்க்கெட் கயவன்` is part of the source stage direction and is retained rather than neutralized.

translation.english_text: Sugar sacks, twenty; mill-cloth pieces, thirty; yarn bales, six; total...
Fifty-six.
Chi, fool, don't I know that! If we calculate the profit, all fifty-six...
notes: The source line trails off after `ஐம்பத்தாறும்`; the English remains incomplete rather than supplying a profit calculation.

translation.english_text: What profit, sir? Even if we sold it right now, we'd get thirty thousand.
Why, won't it do if we sell later? This isn't a brinjal to rot, man—it's a virgin girl.
notes: The source abruptly compares the nonperishable hoarded goods to `கன்னிப் பொண்ணு` (`virgin girl`); the English retains the jarring metaphor rather than rationalizing it.

translation.english_text: You've started selling virgin girls too?
We can sell one, madam! But we can't tie her up in a sack like this.
notes: The source uses singular `அதை`; the second-pass English keeps the joke singular instead of shifting to plural `them`.

translation.english_text: Keep quiet, fool.
Why... he could even tie up the black-market demon in a sack.

Didn't I tie it up before I tied the tali around your neck! You speak of the black market with contempt—everything is money. Avvaiyar sang for gruel; Kambar sang for gold. What is this if not black too?
notes: The line runs from the `tie up` joke into the marriage `தாலி` image and then Narayana Pillai's deliberately self-serving analogy about poets receiving material reward; the English preserves the rhetorical sequence without endorsing or explaining it away.
`ப்ளாக்` is retained as `black` in the closing wordplay rather than expanded into a modern economic argument.

source_locator.description: The Tamil scholar arrives.

translation.english_text: (At this moment the Tamil scholar arrives.)
Narayana Pillaival, I am no longer a Tamil scholar. I work in the detective department. I heard that you have a lot of nool.
notes: The source's `நூல்` sets up a thread/book pun. It is retained as `nool` here so the ambiguity is not destroyed before the later clarification.
The verified source gives the explicit speaker prefix `சி. ஜி. டி.` without its usual colon; the immutable dialogue record preserves that anomaly.

translation.english_text: Harahara, who told you that? Do I have nool? I am an honest merchant, a big man in the town! Head of the Sanmarga Sangam.
notes: Narayana Pillai hears `நூல்` in the commodity/thread sense; `nool` is retained until C.G.T. resolves the pun explicitly.

translation.english_text: Thieving fellows!
Who are you calling thieving fellows?
Boss, I had kept four annas by the well. Someone swiped it and went away.
Get lost, fool.
Quiet, quiet, Narayana Pillaival. I meant not the thread used to weave clothes; nool that gives off the fragrance of knowledge—a book.
notes: The source explicitly resolves the `நூல்` homonym here: weaving thread versus a book/text. `nool` remains in the English sentence at the point of resolution to keep the wordplay visible.
The verified source again gives the explicit `சி. ஜி. டி.` prefix without the usual colon; the exact label remains metadata.

translation.english_text: Books? All right, C.G.T. sir! I have plenty of books! Hey Karuppa, go buy from the shop every book the gentleman asks for and bring them, understand? Then please be off; it's getting late.
notes: Narayana Pillai evades the inquiry by proposing to buy the requested books from a shop; the English keeps the comic evasion without adding an explanation.

translation.english_text: Thank you. Goodbye.
notes: In this departure context, `வணக்கம்` is rendered as `Goodbye` rather than the arrival-oriented `Greetings`.

translation.english_text: My pleasure.

source_locator.description: After leaving Madurai, Kalyani reaches Tiruchi and stands starving near Narayana Pillai's doorway.

translation.english_text: (At this moment Kalyani, having left Madurai, has come to Tiruchi and stands near the entrance of Narayana Pillai's house, suffering from hunger.)
Sir, my child and I are starving—something...
notes: The source trails off after `ஏதாவது`; the English remains incomplete rather than supplying a specific request.

translation.english_text: Why, you've started begging at such a young age? Who are you?
notes: The feminine vocative `ஏம்மா` is not a literal kinship claim; the second-pass English removes the misleading `mother` while preserving the question.

translation.english_text: I'm an orphan. Even if I can get some household work, that's enough.
Then will you work here?
I'm ready, sir.
Hey Karuppa, take her inside.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran reaches Tiruchi after failing to find Kalyani in Madurai, takes Vimala's luggage as if for hire, runs, and escapes with only the food when chased.

notes: The source contains a nested parenthetical ending with `தன் பசியின் கொடுமையை அறிந்து`; the English preserves it as a separate bracketed thought rather than inventing a completed action.
translation.english_text: (After failing to find Kalyani in Madurai, Gunasekaran reaches Tiruchi and is near the railway station. At that moment he takes the luggage of a woman named Vimala, who has arrived by train, saying he will carry it for hire, and runs away. When some people chase him, he takes only the food and runs. [Aware of the cruelty of his hunger.])

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran sits by the well in the rear garden of Vimala's house, eating the stolen food and singing.

translation.english_text: (The man who stole the food sits by the well in the rear garden of Vimala's house, eating it as he sings.)

notes: This is the verified soundtrack occurrence `parasakthi-song-008`; its PDF 31→32 boundary is preserved as one translation unit.
The verified source forms `பட்டி சாதி` and `பட்சமாயிருங்க` remain semantically pressure-sensitive; they are transliterated rather than silently repaired or assigned a more specific meaning.
english_lines: Kaa—kaa—kaa—kaa—
To eat, everyone gather as one;
come running with affection—
to make the lesson of experience clear, O crow-brothers,
with your lovely mouths
you sing a melody—crying kaa, kaa,
you gather together as one—come. (Kaa)
People are suffering without food;
they cry aloud, their hearts in anguish;
when they ask, 'Pour us some gruel-water to save a life,'
look—you bolt the doors.
Where are those cruel ones? Let selfishness leave;
sing that raga upon the earth. (Kaa)
For rice thrown among spit-stained leavings,
beggars fight—on the road;
the weak and the strong,
communal quarrels, money quarrels—
how many in this country.
Let `patti saathi` go—
do not look for our rationalists;
be `patchamāyirunga`; live by sharing what you eat;
do not change that habit—come, sing. (Kaa)

source_locator.description: Vimala is drawn by the song, comes there, and Gunasekaran runs away in fear; she gives him the title Puthumaippithan.

notes: `புதுமைப்பித்தன்` is retained as the source's Tamil title/name rather than replaced with an external literary reference.
translation.english_text: (Drawn there by the charm of the song, Vimala comes over. Seeing her, Gunasekaran runs away in fear. She bestows on him the title 'Puthumaippithan'.)

source_locator.description: At Chandrasekaran's house.

translation.english_text: [At Chandrasekaran's house.]
Father is dead. In the end, my younger sister had to make and sell idlis. When I think of Gnana Sekaran's death, I am afraid.
notes: The second pass renders `ஞான சேகரன் இறந்ததை நினைக்கும்போது` directly as thinking of Gnana Sekaran's death, without adding chronology or cause.

translation.english_text: Do you have their photograph?
There is no photograph of Kalyani. But there is a photograph of Guna Sekaran.

source_locator.description: Black-marketeer Narayana Pillai, described as a tiger in cow's hide, begins his deceitful drama.

translation.english_text: (Black-marketeer Narayana Pillai—a tiger wrapped in a cow's hide—begins his `kuzhuchiyana` deceitful drama.)
notes: The source metaphor `பசுத் தோல் போர்த்திய புலி` is retained literally. The verified source adjective `குழுச்சியான` remains semantically opaque, so the second pass transliterates it rather than silently assigning a specific meaning.

translation.english_text: Why so many books?

They're all for that C.I.D. scholar. He has read everything from the Kanda Puranam in our house to the Sri Valli cinema songbook.
