Now all sorts of things have come out—Kudumba Vilakku, Pandiyan Parisu, Rangoon Radha, Ilatchiya Varalaru—all of it came to fifty rupees... Mm, Kalyani... Kanta—I forgot to tell you. A new film was released today. Its name is Krishna Leela—
notes: Book and film titles are retained in transliteration rather than normalized to later English titles.

translation.english_text: Come, let's go to the second show.
I already saw it at the matinee. You go and see it.
Why should I go?
notes: The verified source form `நானக்குப் போறேன்` is colloquial/opaque; the English keeps the context-based reading without changing Tamil.

translation.english_text: Oh, go. I wouldn't say it without a reason. The love scene in it is terrific. I saw it—will you go and come back?
All right, I'll go and come back.
Hmm—go. Hey, Karuppa, go with madam and come back—
notes: `அம்மா` here is a household address for Kanta; `madam` avoids a misleading literal `mother`.

translation.english_text: Sir, shall I come too?
Get lost, fool!

source_locator.description: Kanta and Karuppan go to the cinema.

translation.english_text: (Kanta and Karuppan go to the cinema.)
[To himself.] Ah, Saturn is finally gone. O helper in distress! Father! Show me a little mercy in the matter of Kalyani. You have done all sorts of things for all sorts of people! Kalyani! Kalyani!
notes: `சனியன்` retains the source's Saturn/nuisance image. `ஆபத்பாந்தவா` is rendered conservatively as `helper in distress` rather than expanded into a stronger theological claim.

translation.english_text: What is it, master?

Kanta has gone off to the cinema on her own. Bring me that water vessel. Second show... mud-clod—she'll come only at twelve. From now on I'll have to call only you whenever something has to be fetched—can you read?
notes: `தண்ணுடையைக்` is rendered contextually as `water vessel`; `மண்ணுங்கட்டி` is retained as the contemptuous aside `mud-clod` rather than omitted.

translation.english_text: I can.
Bravo, bravo! Then read all these books!
notes: The second pass renders the period exclamation `பலே, பலே` by function while preserving its repetition.

translation.english_text: All right, master—.
“A Widow's Love.”
Ah!... [She is startled.]
There's a book like that. Look, some Bharathidasan too has said something about a widow.
notes: The dismissive `யாரோ பாரதிதாசனும்` is retained as character speech, not treated as an archival judgment.

english_lines: Here it lies with no one asking for it, brother—
a jackfruit ripened at the root.
Even a widow, it seems, has love.
Have you ever seen bees that do not sing,
a breeze that does not wander,
or a sound stomach that never hungers?
notes: This is the verified literary quotation `parasakthi-song-009`, explicitly introduced in the source as Bharathidasan; it is not a soundtrack song.

translation.english_text: All right, master. I'm getting sleepy.
I'm not sleepy, though. Kalyani, do you want an unexpected kiss?
notes: `எதிர்பாராத முத்தம்` functions as another suggestive book-title phrase in the surrounding dialogue; the English preserves the literal wording.

translation.english_text: Ah! [She is startled.]

That's a book too. All sorts of things have come out. I'm looking at them just like this. All this travelling by train and car has left my whole body aching, Kalyani. Will you massage my body a little?

english_page_segments.english_text: That's a book too. All sorts of things have come out. I'm looking at them just like this.
All this travelling by train and car has left my whole body aching, Kalyani. Will you massage my body a little?

notes: This immutable dialogue record crosses PDF 33→34 and remains one English unit.

translation.english_text: (She sheds tears.)
Foolish girl! Why, Kalyani! Oh, none of that, amma. Just bring me that pillow.
notes: The feminine vocative ending in `வேண்டாம்மா` is retained as `amma`, not translated as literal kinship `mother`.

source_locator.description: As Kalyani brings the pillow, Narayana Pillai lustfully grabs her hand and pulls her.

translation.english_text: (As she brings it, he lustfully grabs Kalyani's hand and pulls her.)
Master, this does not befit your standing. You are a big man!
That's exactly why I'm behaving like this. You should be proud that a big man is fond of you.
Master! If I had wished, I would have been not a servant in your house—but a lady of rank.
notes: `சீமாட்டி` is rendered as `lady of rank`; the class contrast with household servant is retained.

translation.english_text: What's gone wrong even now! Kalyani—one glance! Just move your eyes; after that, at your feet, this humble one is your lifelong slave.
notes: `சிரஞ்சீவி அடிமை` is rendered as `lifelong slave`, preserving the extravagant submission without importing a modern romantic idiom.

translation.english_text: Chi... lust-demon!
You eat my salt and betray me?
Your salt is for my labour, not for my body. I am a worker employed in your house.
In the inner chambers of great men, there is no room for any question of worker and master.
notes: `அந்தப்புரம்` is translated as `inner chambers`; the source's class/sexual rhetoric is not expanded or softened.

translation.english_text: If you try to touch me, you will see only my corpse.
Then at least give up your life. I'll come touching you at least as far as the cremation ground. Kalyani, you are the mistress of my pleasure.
notes: The source's macabre `சுடுகாடுவரைக்கும்` and `என்னின்ப எஜமாணி` imagery is retained rather than euphemized.

source_locator.description: Narayana Pillai goes to embrace Kalyani.

translation.english_text: (Saying this, he goes to embrace Kalyani.)
Ayyo, Amma... (Kanta arrives.)

A fine display of your character... the big man of the town! You sent me to Krishna Leela and you're staging Narayana Leela here? You've started even with the servant girl? The whole town is laughing itself sick about your body!
notes: The second pass removes the interpretive `bodily escapades` and keeps the compressed source phrase `உடம்பைப் பற்றித்தான் ஊர் சிரிப்பாச் சிரிக்குதே` close to its literal bodily reference.

translation.english_text: You went to the cinema—why are you back here?
Madam came back halfway, master.

source_locator.description: Standalone source text `பாரா-3.` appears before the PDF 35 page boundary.

translation.english_text: [Para-3.]
notes: The canonical scene contains standalone `பாரா-3.`. Its function is not inferred; the English preserves it as a source marker rather than deleting or expanding it.

translation.english_text: Don't I know the story of this Narayana Pillai? That's why even the dolls from the houses next door and opposite are afraid to come!
notes: `பொம்மைகள்` is retained literally as `dolls`; the English does not silently decide whether the source uses it figuratively for women or girls.

translation.english_text: Why would they come here!
Yes! If someone grabbed and dragged your elder or younger sister by the hand like this, would you keep quiet?
I do what I please. Who are you to question me?
Then I too am going to take someone by the hand and drag them away as I please.
Get lost, you mundi—go!
notes: `முண்டி` is an abusive source form whose exact social force remains pressure-sensitive, so it is transliterated rather than normalized.

translation.english_text: Ayyo, what is this, master!
Go, woman, go!
Chi! What kind of man are you! Kalyani, bolt the door properly! Any dog may come barging in!

source_locator.description: Kalyani leaves Narayana Pillai's house.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani leaves that house.)

source_locator.description: Kalyani walks along the street in severe hunger.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani walks along the street, tormented by hunger.)
notes: The second pass keeps the source `பசியால் துடித்துச்` as active suffering from hunger rather than merely a general state of hunger.

english_lines: Is there only hardship for those without means?
Is there no new life?
Is there no path for the darkness to depart?
O Lord, will you not tell me? (Poru)
Is there no one to look upon the face
of one fading from hunger?
Is there no one to protect us?
Is there no compassion to support us poor ones?
Is there no path for the darkness to depart?
O Lord, will you not tell me? (Poru)
Is there no way in this land
to drive away the demon of poverty—to remove it?
In a world where one could say, 'There are none without means'—
where one could say, 'There are none without means'—
is there no such blessed day?
Is there no path for the darkness to depart?
O Lord, will you not tell me? (Poru)
notes: This is the verified soundtrack occurrence `parasakthi-song-010` and remains one single-page semantic-poetic translation unit.
`பொருள்` is rendered contextually as `means` rather than narrowed to cash alone, preserving the song's poverty rhetoric.

source_locator.description: Narayana Pillai and Karuppan are on their way back from the temple.

translation.english_text: (Narayana Pillai and Karuppan are on their way back from the temple.)
Sir! At least give me one of those pieces of coconut! (Karuppan gives one.)
notes: The second pass uses the less specific `piece of coconut` for pressure-sensitive `தேங்காய் முடி`; the embedded giving action belongs to the immutable dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Hey, you arrogant fellow! Why did you give away the coconut?
At the temple sermon they said, 'Charity protects one's head.'
notes: The proverb-like `தர்மம் தலைகாக்கும்` is kept close to its literal image rather than replaced with a modern moral maxim.

translation.english_text: Did they say that at the temple for you and me? That's money, man! Give it here. (He asks for it back.)
notes: The source abruptly invokes `பணம்`; the English preserves that turn rather than supplying an explanation.

translation.english_text: We're poor, master!
Poor... `ezhavu`! (He strikes him.) Hey—dog! You want prasad? (At this moment Gunasekaran arrives.)
notes: The source `ஏழை...ஏழவு` pivots through a sound-play/abusive form. The second pass transliterates `ஏழவு` rather than forcing one lexical sense such as `funeral`.

translation.english_text: Who are you?
Feels like I've seen you somewhere.
You would have, you would have.
You... you...
General Merchant Narayana Pillai.
I... `sermaiya`...
notes: The verified fragment `நானு சேர்மையா...` remains opaque. The second pass transliterates `சேர்மையா` rather than completing it as `chairman` or another guessed word.

translation.english_text: A servant?
You...
The chairman wants to see me?
Yes! Yes! He too, from you...
notes: The source utterance is fragmentary (`அவருகூட உங்ககிட்டே`); the English remains fragmentary rather than repairing the sentence.

translation.english_text: Wants sugar? He needs it by the sackful, doesn't he? Come by our house in the evening; I'll give it secretly.
You'll give it in black?
Hey, what are you?
Then... shall I come in the evening? You'll give it in black?
Come... come.
Then... may I go now?
notes: The second pass preserves the pause in sense without copying the source semicolon into unnatural English punctuation.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran strikes Narayana Pillai.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran strikes Narayana Pillai.)
What is this, man?
This is a beating, man! Hey dog, you want coconut? You want prasad for the poor? Give it here!
notes: Gunasekaran echoes Narayana Pillai's earlier abusive phrasing; the English keeps the repetition visible without adding `meant for` to the compact source phrase.

translation.english_text: Parasakthi! These `ottappa` fellows have come to the point of beating you today.
notes: The colloquial source form `ஒட்டப்பசங்க` remains pressure-sensitive; the second pass transliterates its distinctive element instead of fixing it as `street fellows`.

translation.english_text: If the poor, who have been the ones running, become the ones who kick, then in a moment those who run and those who stand high will all change and become equals—understand that! You'll give it in black? Here, take one in black... (Gunasekaran kicks Narayana Pillai and knocks him down.)
notes: The source builds a rhyming political word-chain `ஓடப்பர் / உதையப்பர் / உயரப்பர் / ஒப்பப்பர்`. The English preserves the semantic progression—running, kicking, high, equal—while documenting that the full sound pattern cannot be reproduced.
The final `ப்ளாக்கிலே` repetition is retained as `in black`; no different pun is invented.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran washes his hands in the river.

translation.english_text: (Gunasekaran, washing his hands in the river.)
Kalyani, at least I steal, deceive and threaten people and manage to eat. What hardships are you and your child going through to satisfy your hunger?

source_locator.description: Vimala, who has got down from a boat on the river, catches hold of Gunasekaran.

translation.english_text: (At that moment Vimala, who has got down from a boat on the river, catches hold of Gunasekaran.)
I'm not a thief! I'm not a thief!

You're no thief at all. I didn't think that. You're taking what your hunger needs and going. If you'd only asked me, I would have given it. If you'd received it and gone, you could simply have walked away.
notes: The last sentence preserves the source contrast between receiving the food and being able to leave by walking, rather than adding an explicit explanation about his earlier flight.

translation.english_text: I thought you'd be just like everyone else.
Is that why you sang, 'Don't look for rationalists'?
notes: This line explicitly refers back to the pressure-sensitive wording of the scene-26 song; the English does not use it to alter that earlier Tamil occurrence.

translation.english_text: Yes. It is wrong to call merciless people rationalists.
Hey, you're quite a clever fellow... who are you?
What am I, the Collector of this town? If you happen to ask, my story itself is a long one.
I like stories very much. Tell me.
You won't be able to enjoy even an atom's worth of this story.
You're only whetting my curiosity more! You absolutely must tell me. Come home.
Home?!
Just come. Don't be afraid. (She takes him along.)
notes: The embedded action is part of the immutable dialogue record and is retained inside the same translation unit.

source_locator.description: A man is feeding biscuits to a dog when Kalyani arrives.

translation.english_text: (A man is feeding biscuits to a dog. Kalyani arrives then.)
Darling...
Sir, my child and I are starving! The child's stomach is burning! Anything—half an anna—to buy milk...
notes: `வயிறு காயுது` is kept as the hunger image `stomach is burning` rather than medically expanded.
The source asks for `ஏதாவது ஒரு அரையணா`; the second pass keeps the open plea first and the half-anna amount second rather than reversing them.

source_locator.description: Source-labelled utterance `ஒரு : போ...போ...` appears between dialogue records d002 and d003 but has no record in the immutable four-record dialogue derivative.

translation.english_text: Go... go...
notes: This explicitly labelled canonical line is translated directly from the verified scene because it is not represented in the immutable scene-32 dialogue-record file. No dialogue ID is invented and the Tamil derivative is not modified.

translation.english_text: Sir, at least give me one of the biscuits you're giving that dog.
What did you say? Did you say 'dog'? This is my darling... go... go...

source_locator.description: At Vimala's house, Gunasekaran tells his story.

translation.english_text: (At Vimala's house, Gunasekaran tells his story.)

I went seeking pearls and ended up picking shells. I dreamed that joy would crawl through my sister's house, enthusiasm would swing there, and delight would coo. But there, anguish came a hundred times a second; cast into poverty, I went there like a madman. In that state, what good would revealing myself do? I must not tell my sister who I am and make her life more painful. She has cried enough. I thought her elder brother need not cry too. But my beloved goddess Kalyani has gone very far, beyond my sight. I search! I search! I keep searching.
notes: `இந்த நிலையில் அறிமுகம் ஒருகேடா?` is rhetorically pressure-sensitive; the first-pass English reads it as questioning the value of revealing his identity without altering the Tamil.

translation.english_text: After hearing your story, I don't know whether to cry or laugh.
Why?
You don't have as much sense as you have love. Don't get angry because I say this. When your wealth was stolen, you should have gone to the police.
I went with a vessel... drank a drink... lost the money. I was ashamed to tell the police about it.
notes: The Tamil builds a sound-chain through `பானை / பானம் / பணம்`; the English keeps the semantic sequence but cannot reproduce the full sound play.

translation.english_text: You wandered as a beggar and felt no shame. You became a thief and still felt no shame. But you were ashamed only to tell others how you were deceived. What a strange man.
You don't know. Society itself is a beggars' monastery, a lunatic asylum, a thieves' cave. Why should I alone be ashamed in it?

Yes! Society is indeed a beggars' monastery. But in it you are a paradesi without a begging bowl. Society is indeed a lunatic asylum; in it you are a madman who does not know `kalveriya`. Society is a thieves' cave; in it you are a thief who does not know how to wield a `kanakkol`. Think about society—`sarasaramai thidukkidave`! Without even realizing it, you have joined society and become a fool along with it.
notes: The verified source forms `கல்வெறியத்`, `கனக்கோல்`, and `சரசாரமாய் திடுக்கிடவே` are pressure-sensitive. The first pass leaves the uncertain portions visibly transliterated rather than silently repairing or over-defining them.

translation.english_text: A fool? Me?
Yes. I'll say it a thousand times. How many people in beggars' clothes are rich...

How many millionaires roam in the guise of madmen. Service to temples, festivals for Tirumal... behind this screen, how many thieves roam. You too changed into a thief... a madman... a beggar. Were you able to attain that enchanting life within yourself?
notes: The source's `இந்தத் திரையிலே` is kept as the image of a screen/cover rather than expanded into an explanatory political gloss.

translation.english_text: What I need is not an enchanting life—Kalyani! My sister Kalyani!

Even now I accuse you of the great fault in your life. You are selfish. You collapsed in anguish over your own sister and her sickly life, but did you ever stop to think how many sisters in this country are wasting away? Out of love and possessive longing for your own sister, when you went seeking work from house to house, you must have seen a woman standing at a doorway, crying in a choking voice, 'Hunger! Hunger!' Who are they all? You keep shouting 'Kalyani! Kalyani!'—not one Kalyani, but a crore Kalyanis, with tears as their blanket, helpless living corpses moving through this country. Has your tongue ever moved for them? Has your heart ever throbbed for them?
notes: The long clause around `அன்பும் பேராசையிலே வேலை வாங்கிக்கொண்டு வீட்டுவாசல்களிலே` is syntactically dense in the verified source. The second pass keeps its sequence as love/longing → seeking work at doorways → encountering the hunger-stricken woman, without repairing the Tamil.

translation.english_text: Why should it beat for me? It should beat for this rotten society, this ungrateful country, for the cheats who live by trampling the poor. Why should heart, life and body all throb for me!
notes: The opening `எனக்கென்ன அடிக்கவேண்டும்?` is read in continuity with the preceding question about the heart beating.

translation.english_text: You too are a part of that society.
But a poor one.
And who made you poor like that? I praise that wandering woman who deceived you and took your money!
notes: `நாட்டோடி` is kept as `wandering woman`. The opening `அப்படி ஆகப்பட்டாய் இதற்கேன்!` is read contextually as asking what/who brought about his poverty, which the following clause answers, without altering the source wording.

translation.english_text: You praise her?

Yes! She is the one who opened your eyes. If you had not become poor, you would not even have thought about the world of the poor. You would not have known that such a world existed. Your world would have been a city of pleasure. You would enjoy the breeze that blows in the palace; you would never see the storm groaning in the hut. You would have learned to hate society's distortions. But you try to put out a volcano by pouring water on it. You play the magudi to tame a mountain snake. Social revolution is not the cutting of a branch of Halahala poison.
notes: The source's mythic and political metaphors—volcano, mountain snake/magudi and `ஆலகால விஷம்`—are retained rather than rationalized.

translation.english_text: It is uprooting its very taproot. Be ashamed. For the things you undertook, the way to end suffering was not the disguises you put on. Those efforts should not have been only for that. They should have been for the thousands upon thousands of suffering sisters. Be ashamed of that, suffer over it, and grieve over it.
Enough! Enough!
Forgive me. I have hurt your mind. We must find a new path to turn the desert into a flower garden. There is no use in scooping up and scattering earth as you do.
notes: `மண்ணைவாரி இறைத்துப்` is retained as the physical image of scooping and scattering earth rather than replaced by a generalized idiom.

translation.english_text: Yes! So the pages of experience in the book of the world are being turned like this. Who is the teacher behind all this?
It is all my elder brother.
notes: The source form `அண்ணு` is resolved contextually as Vimala's elder brother: d026 says she has one and ends `அவர் தங்கை நான்`; the verified character derivative likewise identifies Vimala's elder-brother role without supplying a proper name.

translation.english_text: Your elder brother?

Yes. I told you earlier that I have an elder brother. Our whole family is strange. My father wanders in a contrary world of, 'What does it matter if Rama rules? What does it matter if Ravana rules?' My brother has a mind open to new ideas. I am his sister.
notes: `அண்ணு` is rendered as `elder brother` from the immediate kinship statement `அவர் தங்கை நான்` and the verified character derivative; no proper name is supplied.
`எதிர்த்துலகில்` remains pressure-sensitive and is kept close as `in a contrary world` rather than normalized to a broader political interpretation.

source_locator.description: That night.

translation.english_text: (That night.)
(On the bed.) Kalyani—are you in the forest, or among cattle? And I am here on a cot—che... che... They say that while `Rom nagam` was burning, King Nero was playing the fiddle. Kalyani! Kalyani!
notes: The verified source reads `ரோம் நகமும்`. Because that form is textually fixed but does not parse cleanly, the first pass preserves it as `Rom nagam` rather than silently normalizing the Tamil through a familiar Nero reference.

source_locator.description: Vimala dreams; the following song occurs in the dream.

translation.english_text: (Vimala dreams—in the dream.)

english_lines: You who touch the new bride's heart and go—
tell me your thought before you go.
You who stir this young heart and go—
tell me of that breast before you go. (Pudhu)
Thinking of you everywhere, without telling me,
in the dark hour, unseen by anyone,
stealthily, without making a sound,
without pausing to think over all that had been thought. (Pudhu)
You who flew all around me, don't simply go away;
taste the honey of this brand-new flower before you go.
Why do you break my cherished dream of joy?
Can anyone ever cut the cord of love?
notes: This is verified soundtrack occurrence `parasakthi-song-011`, the primary scene-33 occurrence of soundtrack track 5; it remains distinct from the later reprise in scene 47.
The source forms `அந்த மார்பத்தை` and `என்—இன்பக்கனவை பேணு கலைக்கிறாய்?` are pressure-sensitive. The first-pass semantic rendering stays close to the verified words without repairing them.

source_locator.description: At daybreak.

translation.english_text: (At daybreak.)
Guna! Did you go away thinking I am an idealist? Must the idealist in me be one who rejects love...
notes: The source utterance is deliberately unfinished at the PDF-page boundary and is not fused with the separately labelled next record.

translation.english_text: Why must she be Manimekalai? She can be Kannagi too.
Father's name?
Paramasiva Pillai.
Your name?
Ramachandran.
Ramachandran Pillai...
I don't have any 'pillai' or anything like that, sir.
notes: The source jokes on `பிள்ளை` as name element and child, with reduplicative `பிள்ளை கிண்ணை`; the English preserves the visible wordplay rather than pretending it is ordinary surname confirmation.

translation.english_text: Hey—your caste, man!
notes: The official's `ஜாதி` follows the `பிள்ளை` surname/child joke; the second pass removes the added explanatory verb `I'm asking` and keeps the terse source force.

translation.english_text: That's the very thing that's bad.
Father's occupation?
Temple trustee.
Name?
Sornlal.
(Looking at the next man.) Why did you come here? In Madras there's room for only four people.
Please show a little more heart toward our Delhi man.
notes: `நம்ம டில்லிக்காரனுடைய கொஞ்சம் பெரிய மனசு வையுங்கோ?` is kept as a plea for greater consideration toward the Delhi man, without supplying unstated administrative context.

translation.english_text: When are you ever going to reach Delhi?

source_locator.description: Gnana Sekaran arrives with a lame leg.

translation.english_text: (Gnana Sekaran arrives with a lame leg.)
Sir...
Go... go... there's no room.
We're a whole group...
There's no room even for one... go, sir. It's a complete nuisance.
Then where are all of us to go?
Have you come asking me to show you the way? Go fall somewhere and die.

Even after my leg broke, it was because we feared death that for many months we starved, endured untold suffering, slept by the roadside hungry and walked here. If we were going to die, had we stood our ground in Burma without fearing the bombing, ten thousand of us could have been shot dead as one group. But we did not come to ask for a way to die; we came seeking peace for our distressed minds, which have nowhere to turn.
notes: The closing source syntax `சாவதற்கு வழிகேட்க வழியில்லா...` is dense; the first pass preserves the contrast between being told to die and coming to seek peace rather than smoothing it into a new argument.

translation.english_text: Sattam! Is this an office, or your house?
notes: The verified exclamation `சட்டம்!` is retained as `Sattam!` because its exact force in this utterance is pressure-sensitive.

translation.english_text: There is no room—no room for genuine refugees. In a land that welcomed all who came, there is no room for one born here. As long as heartless people like you exist, there is no room even for human beings; there is no room for love, for virtue—for any of them.

english_page_segments.english_text: There is no room—no room for genuine refugees. In a land that welcomed all who came,
there is no room for one born here. As long as heartless people like you exist, there is no room even for human beings; there is no room for love, for virtue—for any of them.

notes: This immutable dialogue record crosses PDF 41→42 and remains one English unit.

translation.english_text: Get out! Get out!
A charity shop is named Karunai Mahal; this place is named a refugee camp. Come, we'll go.
notes: The `கருணை / கருணைமகால்` wording is retained as the source's ironic naming contrast rather than explained away.

translation.english_text: Rather than wandering like this, we might as well go to prison.

source_locator.description: Long source-labelled Gnana Sekaran speech after dialogue record d056, including the beggars' conference proposal and embedded crowd reactions; it is present in the verified scene but absent from the immutable 56-record dialogue derivative.

translation.english_text: Wait, brother. If, without thinking anything through clearly, four people do something in anger, then prison is where we will have to go. The world does not know our condition. We are not the only beggars; beggars are spread throughout this whole country. First we must bring all the beggars together. It does not seem that either the government or the national parties are working for us. Rather than go door to door publishing our demands, it is better to spread them through the country. There is no merit in our voice merely reaching the Collector; it must reach the government. We must unite all the beggars and hold a conference. It must be called the Madras Province Beggars' Conference. (Everyone laughs.) Why are you laughing? I didn't say it to make you laugh. Think about it. The resolution to emerge there should be that we demand voting rights. Once we obtain that, we can all stand for election together. No one will dare contest against us. The resolutions passed at our conference must be carried out. We must make even the `paradesi` government that we `ottugira` tremble. (Even if it costs our lives, we must raise our voice for our rights loudly. We must shape a path by which our future society can live in prosperity, the group shouted.)
notes: This explicitly labelled canonical block is translated directly from the verified scene because it is not represented in the immutable scene-33 dialogue-record file. No dialogue ID is invented and the Tamil derivative is not modified.
The voting-rights sequence supports `கூட நிற்கலாம்` as standing for election together because it is immediately followed by `எதிர்த்து போட்டியிட`; this contextual clarification does not alter Tamil.
The phrase `நாம் ஓட்டுகிற பரதேசி அரசாங்கத்தையே` remains pressure-sensitive. The second pass still keeps `paradesi` and `ottugira` visible rather than choosing an unsupported meaning for that phrase.

source_locator.description: Location: refugee camp.

translation.english_text: (Location: refugee camp.)
Brother, I hear all the refugees have come from Rangoon!
notes: `அண்ணு` is treated here as a generic kinship/respect address (`brother`), not as a proper name.

translation.english_text: Yes. Who do you want?
Chandrasekaran, Gnana Sekaran, Guna Sekaran.
There is no one by those names! There's a group under that banyan tree—go and inquire there.
Brother, you all came from Burma, didn't you?
notes: The repeated `அண்ணு` is again rendered as a generic address (`brother`), not a personal name.

translation.english_text: Yes, amma. We came as refugees and turned into mendicants!
notes: `ஆண்டிகள்` is rendered as `mendicants`, preserving the descent from refugee status without importing a modern institutional category.

translation.english_text: Did you know my elder brothers in Rangoon?
`Oorum.` What are their names?
notes: The verified source begins with the pressure-sensitive form `ஊரும்.`. The second pass leaves it transliterated rather than silently correcting or guessing its function.

translation.english_text: Chandrasekaran... Gnana Sekaran... Guna Sekaran...
This is our whole group—only this many people. Look and see whether your brothers are among them. (Kalyani looks; they are not.)
notes: The embedded action belongs to the immutable dialogue record and remains within the same translation unit.

source_locator.description: Hunger torments Kalyani and she begs.

translation.english_text: (Tormented by hunger, Kalyani begs.)
Sir, it has been six days since my child and I ate.

notes: The contrast between public begging and concealed hunger inside the house is preserved without adding a broader social explanation.
translation.english_text: It has been three days since we ate. You go street to street asking for alms; we stay inside the house. That is the difference. Today there is a feast at Judge Sekar's house. Go ask there.
Which house, sir?
There, you can see it—that house on the corner.

source_locator.description: Kalyani leaves.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani leaves.)

source_locator.description: The lame man who had gone outside returns.

notes: The source role label `நொண்டி` is descriptive; the English stage direction does not use later continuity to assign a personal identity.
translation.english_text: (The lame man, who had gone outside, returns.)

notes: The vocative source form `இராகவா` is transliterated as `Iragava` rather than normalized to a nominative personal name.
translation.english_text: Iragava, is there anything special today?

notes: The verified source opens with `பாலம்`, retained as `Baalam` rather than silently corrected.
The form `இரங்கூனிலேன்னுமன்று` is pressure-sensitive; the surrounding syntax supports the Rangoon/brothers question, but the Tamil itself is not repaired.
translation.english_text: Baalam. A beggar woman came with a child. She asked who all of us were. We said we had been earning in Rangoon and were coming back... She asked whether we knew her elder brothers in Rangoon. We said we didn't.
What did she say her name was?

notes: The apparent mismatch with the following names is retained from the verified source rather than reconciled.
translation.english_text: That doesn't even seem like a Tamil Nadu name, does it?
Something like—Chandrasekaran...
Did she say Chandrasekaran, Gnana Sekaran, Guna Sekaran?
Yes...

notes: The embedded fall is part of the immutable dialogue record and remains inside the same English unit.
translation.english_text: Ayyo, Kalyani! My younger sister Kalyani! Kalyani! (Crying out, he falls down.)

source_locator.description: At Chandrasekaran's house, Kalyani begs.

translation.english_text: (At Chandrasekaran's house, Kalyani begs.)
Sir! My child and I are starving.
All right, come later!
Sir, may you live well!
Don't you understand when you're told once?

notes: `கோடி புண்ணியம்` is kept as religious merit rather than converted into a material reward.
translation.english_text: Sir, a crore-fold merit to you...

source_locator.description: Kalyani catches hold of Sekar's feet.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani catches hold of Sekar's feet.)

notes: `புண்ணியம் பார்த்துப் பார்த்துத்தான்` is rhetorically pressure-sensitive; the English keeps the repeated merit wording rather than supplying an unstated explanation.
The kick is embedded in the immutable dialogue record and remains inside the same unit.
translation.english_text: It is by looking after merit again and again that I have ended up unable even to see my younger sister's face. (Saying this, he kicks Kalyani away.)

notes: The invective preserves the source's sibling appeal, hunger image, `பரட்டைத் தலை`, cotton-in-the-eyes metaphor, and `பாவம்... புண்ணியம்... நாசம்` sequence without smoothing them into a new argument.
translation.english_text: Ah, sinners! Were you people not born with brothers and sisters? Even after seeing my little child writhing with hunger, even after seeing this dishevelled head—sinners! Have your eyes been stuffed with cotton? O embodiments of non-violence who speak of sin... merit... ruin—if there is such a thing as ruin, that alone will be the fitting place for you. It will be the fitting place for you.

source_locator.description: Kalyani is driven away by the servant.

translation.english_text: (Kalyani is driven away by the servant.)

notes: The source's `உன் அப்பாவும் மாமாவும் இருந்தால் நீதான் உன் அப்பாவை கர்ப்பத்திலே விழுங்கி விட்டாயே` is left structurally close and deliberately not rationalized into a biographical explanation.
The source says that both mother and child were beaten; the English retains that wording even though the immediately preceding visible action explicitly kicks Kalyani.
translation.english_text: Dear child! This world submits to pomp and wickedness! There is no place for us to live in this world. What are you looking at? Are you looking to see whether the tears running from my eyes might be milk? Your father should have seen you and me being beaten; your maternal uncles should have seen it. If your father and uncles were here... you yourself swallowed your father in the womb! My beauty? Are you hungry? Don't cry. I myself cannot bear the hunger; how can I bear your voice? Come, let's go.

source_locator.description: Gunasekaran, after wandering in search of his sister, expresses his anguish through song.

translation.english_text: (After wandering in search of his sister, Gunasekaran expresses his anguish through song.)

notes: This is verified soundtrack occurrence `parasakthi-song-012`, soundtrack track 3, spanning PDF 44→45 as one translation unit.
The English is derived only from the verified booklet occurrence; it does not substitute a familiar published English rendering of the Bharati poem.
`துஞ்சுது முகட்டிலென்பார்` is kept close as a rooftop/sleeping image rather than normalized beyond the source.
english_lines: My heart cannot bear it—when I think
of these degraded people. (Nenju)
They die fearing and fearing—
there is nothing on earth they do not fear.
They call them deceitful ghosts—
say one is in this tree, in that pond,
say it sleeps on the rooftop—
they suffer greatly, thinking and fearing. (Nenju)
They have no gruel to drink—
nor the knowledge to say what its causes are.
'Famine, famine,' they cry—every day,
suffering, their lives trembling and trembling,
they sleep and die—
and there is no way to end their sorrows. (Nenju)

translation.english_text: Brother, everything you sang is right.

notes: The source itself repeats `பாட` in a way that sounds odd after Gunasekaran has just performed the song. The English keeps that source wording and does not silently replace it with `wrote` or `composed`.
translation.english_text: I didn't sing this song, Kuppa. If I had sung this song, everyone would come to beat me. Someone else sang it.

notes: The source term `தீவெட்டி` remains transliterated as `theevetti` because the verified scene does not define it more precisely; the embedded departure remains within the dialogue unit.
translation.english_text: Hey, Kuppa, it's time for the `theevetti` puja. Come ring the bell. (Gunasekaran leaves.)
What, brother! You're leaving? Will you come tomorrow?

source_locator.description: Kalyani arrives after the puja is over.

translation.english_text: (After the puja is over, Kalyani arrives.)

notes: `லோகமாதா` is retained as `Lokamata` rather than expanded beyond the source address.
translation.english_text: (Facing the idol.) Mother! Parasakthi! You alone are my refuge! Lokamata, save me.
Who is it?
The one without refuge is named Kalyani.

notes: The long source record contains its own stage actions and internal monologue; all remain inside this single immutable dialogue-linked unit.
The source sequence `வழி பலாத்காரம் பலாத்காரமா?` is kept as a broken self-questioning movement rather than rewritten into smoother exposition.
The verified phrase around `சுட்டகல்லில் சோறு ... ஏமாற்றினைப்` is pressure-sensitive; the English keeps the literal fired-stone/rice image and does not repair the Tamil.
translation.english_text: Don't worry, amma. You have come to Ambal's temple precisely so that all your troubles may end. Why are you like this now! Go inside and worship my mother freely, amma! (Kalyani goes inside. As soon as she has gone, the priest says to himself:) Aha! What beauty, what a body! What allure! I must not let her go today. The way? Force. Rape? In Parasakthi's temple? Yes—where else to do it? Priest, after deceiving devotees with talk of 'rice on a fired stone,' rape too? Yes. What is wrong in doing this? Why—are you looking to see whether Ambal is there? She will stay only in this place. She will not walk about. Hmm... don't delay. (Taking Kalyani's hand.) Kalyani, don't think of it differently. Just as a doctor has the right to touch women who are ill... likewise we, as servants of God, have the right to touch women who are devout.
Fie... demon of lust—Mother Parasakthi!

source_locator.description: The priest tries to crush Kalyani's chastity; Kuppan sees it and rings the bell, and she escapes like a spotted deer from a tiger's jaws.

notes: The final animal image is the source's metaphor and is retained without adding an identification gloss.
translation.english_text: (The priest tries to crush Kalyani's chastity. But Kuppan sees this and rings the bell. The spotted deer escapes from the tiger's jaws.)

source_locator.description: Driven by troubles, cruel hunger, and villains who plunder maidens' chastity, Kalyani has reached the very edge of her life.

translation.english_text: (Driven by troubles, the cruelty of hunger, and villains who plunder maidens' chastity, Kalyani has reached the very edge of her life.)

notes: The source's `உலகத்தின் பெயரைச் சொல்லி ... அம்மா என்று கொஞ்சுகிறாயா?` is syntactically and rhetorically pressure-sensitive; the English keeps the world/`Amma` sequence without supplying a psychological explanation.
`திசைகாட்டி? அதுவே என் சகம் காட்டி!` contains the verified pressure-sensitive form `சகம்`; `sagam kaatti` remains transliterated rather than silently repaired.
`சொரணையற்றவர்கள்` is rendered broadly as lacking the sense to give food; the verified source does not support a narrower repair.
`கன்னித்தமிழே` is retained as `Kannithamizh` as a source endearment rather than expanded into an external cultural gloss.
translation.english_text: Dear child! There is the path to our world. If we go to that world, there will be no hunger! Are you trying to take my life by uttering the name of this world—cooing 'Amma'? No. I am going to kill the very life for whose sake I carried this ruined life. I cannot leave you to live alone in this deceitful world. Jewel crawling in my lap, I am going to leave you to crawl in this river. A guide to the way? That itself is my `sagam kaatti`! I am going to send you along the path this river shows. Those without even the sense to give food have at least cut this river for people to fall into and die! Come, let us go to a place without poverty. Give me your last kiss! Won't you? Kannithamizh, give me one tight kiss. Give your last kiss on these dried lips! Give it. Give it.

source_locator.description: Kalyani throws the child into the river; police arrive, pursue her as she jumps into the river, and capture her.

notes: The source action order is preserved without adding outcome details not printed in this scene.
translation.english_text: (Kalyani lifts the child and throws it into the river. At that moment the police arrive and pursue Kalyani; she too jumps into the river, and the police take her into custody.)

notes: The source's diamond-and-sledgehammer image is retained even though the physical metaphor is unusual.
translation.english_text: Death would be far better than suffering like this. Like a sledgehammer blow falling on a diamond, our family has crumpled and shattered. Where has Kalyani gone? What became of my brothers? Gnana Sekaran! Chandrasekaran!

source_locator.description: Location: courtroom; Kalyani is in the accused's dock.

translation.english_text: (Location: courtroom. Kalyani is in the accused's dock.)
(Looking at Kalyani.) What do you say about this killing?
(Silence.)

notes: The source's `உண்மையாக நடந்தால் நிரபராதியாகிவிட முடியாது` is retained as a direct warning rather than expanded into legal explanation.
translation.english_text: If you remain silent like this, it amounts to contempt of court! You stand accused of murder and attempted suicide. If what happened is true, you cannot become innocent. Answer! Who are you? What is your name? What is your native place? Why did you have to kill the child? Who is the child's father? Is it a child whose father's name is unknown?

notes: The reply preserves the source's wordplay between the court asking whether the father's name is unknown and an infant itself not knowing its father's name.
translation.english_text: Yes, it is unknown! How can an infant know its father's name? Your Honour, don't keep asking everything over and over. Just pronounce the judgment.
How can I pronounce judgment without an inquiry, amma?
What do you say about the charges made against you?
What am I to say? Do whatever your law says.
You are a murderer, aren't you?
Yes! According to your law; not according to justice.
Is killing the child you bore what you call justice?
I gave birth; I myself destroyed. Just as there is a right to give birth, there is a right to destroy.
All things that are created belong to the government.

notes: The repeated `சொந்தம்` is preserved as the government's claim of ownership/belonging; the source's rhetorical turn is not replaced by a legal gloss.
translation.english_text: Belong? We struggled for food. We wandered seeking comfort. We were treated worse than mangy dogs. We cried in panic, 'Hunger, hunger'; we writhed like worms of starvation; we sagged and twisted. Then the government did not claim us as its own and support us. What an astonishing government! When we dared to die, it stretches out the hand called law and speaks the crooked word 'ownership'! An astonishing government—wonderful justice.
Don't talk like a child. Do you admit that killing the child was a crime or not?

notes: Nallathangal and Siruthondar are retained as source names; no external retelling is inserted.
translation.english_text: A crime! If this is a crime, how great a crime was it when Nallathangal threw seven children into a well? The story of Nallathangal is performed across the country—why did the law not stop it? You proudly speak of Siruthondar, who cooked his child as meat—why was that not stopped? I only did the lesson they taught. How is this a crime?
Do not speak here by citing Nallathangal and Siruthondar as reasons. Your anger must not insult justice. You are to state only what happened; it is not proper to blame the government or society.

notes: The source describes the child moving aside Kalyani's upper cloth; the English does not add an explicit nursing action beyond what the text states.
translation.english_text: My little child was frantic with hunger. Shamelessly I say this, thinking of everyone here as brothers. My child's tongue would go dry and he would move aside my upper cloth; would this wretched woman, starved for many days, have milk? I could not bear that cruelty. I killed him. Is this a crime?
The child must be saved somehow.

notes: The source's `விஷம் பிடித்தவளாக` and the transition into the repeated `விபச்சாரியாக` are pressure-sensitive; the English stays structurally close rather than repairing the phrasing.
translation.english_text: Is my child Tirugnanasambandar, for Parvati to come and give him milk and save him? I alone had to save him. There were obstacles in my life that would not let me live. Because I did not fall into the net of deceivers, I stand before the law as a criminal. But if only I had moved my body a little, I would be strolling on an upper storey—not as a widow, not as a woman seized by poison. As a prostitute! As a prostitute! That is what this society wants. That is how one can stand against this society. How else can an orphan live?
Are you an orphan?
Yes. Time made me an orphan.
Don't tell stories. State the matter.

notes: The judge's collapse is embedded in the immutable dialogue record and remains inside this unit.
translation.english_text: My mother died the day after I was born. I grew under my father's shadow. I had three elder brothers; I hardly even saw them properly. They went to Rangoon when I was that young. I was married. My husband died; my father too died. I waited with my eyes fixed on the road, thinking my elder brothers Chandrasekaran, Gnana Sekaran and Guna Sekaran would return from Rangoon. My brothers did not come. Carrying my child, I wandered as a beggar. The answer I received in this country was only, 'Get lost, you idle woman.' A judge, they say, a man who practises honesty—he kicked me with his boot when I went to beg. (Judge Sekar realizes that Kalyani is his sister; shocked, he falls down.)

source_locator.description: A preacher speaks on the road.

translation.english_text: (A preacher speaks on the road.)

notes: This immutable dialogue record crosses PDF 48→49 and remains one English unit.
The phrase around `கோவில்புரம் நிறைய நண்பர்களே` is pressure-sensitive in the verified source; the English keeps the temple-town/friends sequence without silently rewriting the Tamil.
`கோமேதகம்` is retained as `gomethagam` rather than assigned an external gemological gloss.
translation.english_text: Cleopatra, the world's great beauty, is said to have put the pearls of Tamil Nadu into liquor and drunk them. Yet the women of such a Tamil land lie starving, waiting for money sent by men who have gone to Rangoon and Singapore to earn. Temples are here. For God there is diamond armour and a gem-studded throne; the dear children of that God suffer even for half a stomach of gruel. The temple town is full, friends, with the cry that a mother sold her child. Because of the cruelty of hunger, many mothers are said to have sold their children. A mother sold her child! The mother who carried it for ten months and suffered every hardship; the mother who cherished and fondled it as she raised it; the mother who laid it in a cradle and sang 'aararo'; the mother who dreamed of feeding milk-rice from a silver bowl to the child crawling along the veranda; the mother who bathed him in turmeric water, heard his baby speech and longed to see his back as she said, 'Go to school, my dear'; the mother who yearned for the day when she would arrange her son's marriage and her son and daughter-in-law would go to the bridal bed—she is said to have sold the child she bore, the diamond that lay in her womb, the `gomethagam`, the golden platter, because of poverty. I tell you: 'Child, child!'—as greens are cried out in the market—eight rupees for a child! A big child five rupees; an infant three rupees. Cruelty! Cruelty!

translation.english_text: The court has encountered many cases full of strangeness; it has seen novel people. So this case is not strange, nor am I, the one arguing it, a novel man. I am a being commonly seen on the road of life. I created confusion in the temple; I attacked the priest. I stand accused. You may expect me to say all this and then deny it; I am not going to deny any of it! Certainly not! I created confusion in the temple—not because there should be no temple, but because a temple should not become a den of the cruel. I attacked the priest, not because he is a devotee, but to condemn devotion becoming a daytime disguise. You may ask, 'Why do you care so much—a concern no one else in the world has?' I myself was affected, directly affected! You may call it selfishness; public good is mixed into my selfishness. A fish eats filth for food and cleans the pond—like that. You call me criminal, criminal; if you walk a little way backward along this criminal's path of life, you can count how many wild rivers he has crossed. There were no singing cuckoos on my path; hooded snakes have writhed there. I have not touched the breeze, but I have crossed fire. Hear my story, Your Honour; please hear it before writing judgment! I was born in Tamil Nadu, here in Thirukkuvalai. One country to be born in, another to survive in—is my fate an exception to Tamil Nadu's fate? Rangoon nurtured my life; it raised me up. I came to see my sister in bridal adornment. Through a fraud case, here I stand before you in the accused's dock. This trickster Jolly—I too was one of those who fell into her net. I lost my cash box. I grew thin with hunger, weakened, and finally became mad. I saw the sister I had come to see—as a painting without eyes. Yes, a widow. My sister's name is Kalyani—an auspicious name! But there is no mangalyam at her neck. A flourishing family had fallen apart. A child in her hand! Tears in her eyes! Kalyani wandered; I wandered for Kalyani. Many showed Kalyani compassion. Among them were some young bulls who asked for her love. This cruel Venu, who stands before you implicated in a murder case, tried through his showiness to violate my sister. Had I not stopped him, Kalyani would have killed herself then. Devotees of God too came forward to show Kalyani compassion; in return they asked for her sidelong glance. The fiercest among them was this priest. He asked for Kalyani's chastity as an offering—in the name of Parasakthi, in the name of the Mother of the World. Kalyani might at least have remained alive, writhing like a worm in this world. It was this priest who drove her to dare suicide. She did not wish to leave her child behind in this merciless world. She did not wish to see her child die writhing without support. She herself killed it. Killing those one loves is no wonder. Gandhi, the world's noble one, embodiment of non-violence and compassion for life, is said to have told them to kill a calf writhing in disease because he could not bear to see it suffer. Kalyani used that same method. How is this a crime? A Tamil returning from abroad has no right to live; a woman born in Tamil Nadu has no suitable protection in which to live. Yet if my sister had yielded a little—if for one day in a millionaire's bedchamber she had named a price for her honour, if for one day in a mansion-dweller's lap she had carried on like this before the country—is that what this court wants? Showiness threatened my sister—she ran in fear. Money chased my sister—she ran again. Devotion frightened my sister—she ran, ran, to the very edge of life. That flight should have been stopped; her suffering should have been relieved. Did those who extend the law today do it? Did they let my Kalyani live?

The English remains semantic-poetic and does not invent rhyme or metre.
`முத்தம்மா` is retained as `Muthamma`; `இல்லாதார் / உள்ளார்` is rendered through the have-not/have contrast without importing outside ideology.
english_lines: Everyone must live—all lives
must dwell in happiness.
This is the thought of good people—Muthamma;
this indeed is the life of good virtue. (Ello)
No one called uneducated among us
should remain.
Non-killing must be cherished; people
must live cooperatively. (Ello)
If there is one who created the have-nots,
let that one perish.
If there are those who have not and those who have—Muthamma,
why these differences? (Ello)
